chapters.title: The data you have and the data you want
chapters.body:
A labeled dataset for an NLP task usually runs to a few thousand examples. Plain running text runs to billions of words. [[transfer-learning|Transfer learning]] is the practice of spending the second on the first: train a model where the data is plentiful, then reuse its parameters where it is not.

By 2018 the field had a working version of that practice. [[language-model-pre-training|Language model pre-training]] trains a model to predict text from text, so [[unlabeled-text|plain text with no annotation]] supplies the entire training signal. The trained weights are then carried over to a [[downstream-task|labeled end task]] that has far less data of its own.

The end tasks come in two shapes, and the difference matters for everything that follows. [[sentence-level-tasks|Sentence-level tasks]] want one label for the whole input, as in [[natural-language-inference|deciding whether one sentence follows from another]]. [[token-level-tasks|Token-level tasks]] want an output at every position, as in [[named-entity-recognition|marking which tokens belong to a name]].

What pre-training produced had also been changing. Instead of one fixed vector per word type, models had begun to produce [[contextual-representations|vectors that depend on the sentence the word appears in]].

The paper sorts all of this prior work into [[transfer-strategies|two strategies]]. The [[feature-based-approach|feature-based]] one freezes the pre-trained model and hands its vectors to an architecture built for the task, as extra input features; [[elmo|ELMo]] is the paper's example. The [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuning]] one adds almost no new weights and trains every pre-trained parameter further on the labeled data; [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] is the example.

Then comes the objection the rest of the paper is built on. Both strategies pre-train with the same kind of objective, and that objective reads a sentence in one direction only.

[[bert|BERT]] is the paper's proposal for lifting that restriction while staying on the fine-tuning route. It claims state-of-the-art results on eleven tasks, each obtained by adding a single output layer to the same pre-trained encoder. [[theme-pre-training-and-how-it-was-reused|The practice being inherited]] is worth seeing in full before the objection lands.

chapters.title: Only one side of the sentence
chapters.body:
A [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]] assigns probability to text by predicting each token from the tokens before it. Nothing to the right of position $i$ may enter the computation that predicts position $i$. In a Transformer that rule is enforced by masking attention, so each token attends only to its own left.

The consequence is about representations, not just about probabilities. If the model is later reused as an encoder, every token's vector was built from half of its sentence.

One obvious repair is to train the mirror image as well. A [[right-to-left-language-model|right-to-left model]] predicts each token from what follows it, and the two models' outputs can be joined per position. That is [[shallow-concatenation|shallow concatenation]], and it is what ELMo does: the two directions never condition on each other during training, and meet only at the end.

The paper names the general problem the [[unidirectionality-constraint|unidirectionality constraint]], and says it also limits which architectures can be pre-trained at all.

Section 5.1 gives [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|three reasons]] for not taking the concatenation route. It costs twice as much as one model. It is awkward for [[question-answering|question answering]], since the right-to-left half cannot condition an answer on a question that sits to its left. And it is strictly weaker than a model that uses both sides at every layer.

That third point is the paper's target. [[deep-bidirectionality|Deep bidirectional representations]] are ones where every layer conditions jointly on left and right, rather than two one-directional stacks glued together at the top. Related work had trained on both sides before at the level of a single word, as [[context2vec|context2vec]] did with LSTMs.

[[fig-3|The three-model diagram]] states the claim as arrows: only BERT has arrows entering a position from both sides at every layer. It is a picture of connectivity, not evidence about quality, and the evidence comes much later. [[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison|The appendix comparison]] also lists differences between BERT and GPT that are not architectural at all — corpus, batch size, which special tokens are learned during pre-training. [[theme-the-one-direction-problem|The one-direction problem]] and [[etheme-two-routes-one-direction|the way it cuts across both transfer routes]] are set out in full there.

chapters.title: One stack, used twice
chapters.body:
[[bert-framework|BERT's framework]] has two steps and one network. Step one pre-trains on [[unlabeled-text]]. Step two initializes a task model with those exact weights and trains all of them on labeled data.

[[fig-1|The two-panel figure]] is the claim in picture form: the same token-in, vector-out encoder appears on both sides, and the dotted arrows carry every pre-trained weight across. What differs between the panels is the thin output layer on top.

Fine-tuning produces [[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task|a separate model per task]], all branching from one checkpoint. The paper calls the small gap between pre-trained and downstream architecture a distinctive feature, and gives it a name: [[unified-architecture-across-tasks|a unified architecture across tasks]].

[[bert-model-architecture|The architecture itself]] is a multi-layer bidirectional [[transformer-encoder|Transformer encoder]]. The paper declines to describe it, says its implementation is almost identical to the original, and points readers at Vaswani et al. So everything about blocks, heads and feed-forward layers is imported rather than restated.

One thing is restated, because it is the whole difference. [[self-attention|Self-attention]] forms each position's next representation as a weighted combination of the positions it is allowed to attend to. BERT allows all of them, in both directions, at every layer, which the paper calls [[bidirectional-self-attention|bidirectional self-attention]]. GPT allows only the left, which it calls [[constrained-self-attention|constrained self-attention]]. Same operation, different mask.

Sizes get a shorthand: [[model-size-notation|$L$ layers, hidden size $H$, $A$ attention heads]]. [[hidden-size-h|$H$]] is the width of the vectors passed between layers, and [[feed-forward-filter-size|each block's feed-forward network is four times that wide]] — 3072 when $H=768$, 4096 when $H=1024$.

[[bert-base-and-bert-large|Two configurations are reported]]. BERT_BASE is $L=12$, $H=768$, $A=12$, at 110M parameters. BERT_LARGE is $L=24$, $H=1024$, $A=16$, at 340M.

The smaller number is not an accident. [[gpt-size-match|BERT_BASE was built at GPT's size on purpose]], so that a later gap between them cannot simply be charged to capacity. [[theme-one-architecture-two-stages|The architecture and its two stages]] are laid out there.

chapters.title: One input format for every task
chapters.body:
A single text, a pair of texts, and a question with the passage that answers it are three different shapes. Designing one encoder for all of them means designing one token format that carries all three. That is what [[input-representation|the input/output representation]] does.

First, a definition that is easy to misread. In this paper [[sentence-as-arbitrary-span|a "sentence" is any contiguous span of text]], not a linguistic sentence, and a "sequence" is the token sequence actually fed to BERT — which may hold one span or two.

Text enters as [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]] subwords, with a [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|vocabulary of 30,000 pieces]]. Rare words are split into known fragments, so nothing is out of vocabulary, and that same 30,000 fixes the width of the prediction layer used in pre-training.

Every sequence opens with [[cls-token|the [CLS] token]]. Its final hidden vector, written [[final-hidden-vector-c|$C$]], is used as the aggregate representation of the whole input. [[sep-token|A [SEP] token]] closes each span, so [[sentence-pair-packing|two spans can be packed into one sequence]] as A and B.

Marking which span a token belongs to is done in the embeddings rather than the architecture. Each token's input vector is [[input-embedding-sum|a sum of three learned vectors]]: the token embedding, a [[segment-embeddings|segment embedding]] saying A or B, and a [[position-embeddings|position embedding]] saying where in the sequence it sits.

[[fig-2|The figure]] draws exactly that, as three rows joined by plus signs. Note that positions are learned rows in a table, not a fixed function of the index, which is why the maximum length is a hard ceiling and why the training schedule later has to reach it.

Two outputs get names here because every head in the paper reads one of them. $C$ is the vector above [CLS], and [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]] is the top-layer vector above token $i$; both live in $\mathbb{R}^H$. Sentence-level heads read $C$, token-level heads read the $T_i$. [[theme-what-bert-reads|The input format]] and [[etheme-one-encoder-one-input-format|the argument that it is what unifies the tasks]] go further.

chapters.title: Hiding words to train on both sides
chapters.body:
You cannot simply train an ordinary language model to look both ways. The paper's reason is [[see-itself-problem|the "see itself" problem]].

Walk it through. If attention is unmasked, then at layer 1 every position's vector already mixes in the token at position $i$. The prediction for position $i$ is computed at the top of the stack from those lower-layer vectors. So the answer reaches its own prediction through the layers below, and the model can get it right without learning anything.

Masking cuts that path by removing the token from the input. That is [[masked-language-model|the masked LM objective]]: choose [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% of the WordPiece positions in each sequence at random]], replace them with [[mask-token|a [MASK] placeholder]], and predict what was there. The final vector at a masked position is fed through [[mlm-output-softmax|an output softmax over the 30,000 pieces]] and trained with cross-entropy against the original token.

The paper notes this is the old [[cloze-task|cloze task]] under a new name. It also marks one difference from [[denoising-autoencoder-contrast|denoising autoencoders]]: only the masked positions are predicted, not the whole input.

Masking buys bidirectional training, and it costs two things. The first is [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning]], because [MASK] appears constantly during pre-training and never once downstream.

[[masking-recipe-80-10-10|The 80/10/10 recipe]] is the mitigation. Of the 15% chosen for prediction, 80% become [MASK], 10% become a random token, and 10% are left exactly as they were — and in all three cases the original token is the target. In whole-corpus terms that is 12% of tokens replaced by [MASK], 1.5% corrupted, and 1.5% predicted in place. The model therefore cannot tell from the input whether a given position is a target, so it has to keep a usable representation of every token.

The second cost is speed. [[mlm-convergence-cost|Only 15% of positions produce a gradient signal per batch]], against every position for a left-to-right model, and the paper reports that it does converge slightly slower. [[etheme-masking-buys-bidirectionality|Masking as the price of bidirectionality]] is the argument in one place.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: The second task, and the run
chapters.body:
Masked prediction is about one span of text. [[question-answering]] and inference are about the relation between two, which a language modelling objective does not directly train.

So BERT is pre-trained on a second task at the same time. [[next-sentence-prediction|Next sentence prediction]] is a binary question: did span B actually follow span A in the corpus? The labels are [[isnext-notnext|IsNext when it did, and NotNext when B was drawn at random from elsewhere]], generated 50/50 from any monolingual text. The decision is read off $C$, and the paper reports the final model getting the task right 97-98% of the time.

A footnote attaches a caution to that. Because $C$ was trained this way, [[c-not-a-sentence-representation|it should not be treated as a general sentence embedding without fine-tuning]].

The paper also marks what it thinks separates this from earlier sentence-relation objectives: [[full-parameter-transfer-vs-sentence-embeddings|those transferred a sentence vector downstream, while BERT transfers every parameter]].

[[pre-training-procedure|The run itself]] is stated plainly. [[pre-training-data|The corpus]] is [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus at 800M words]] plus [[english-wikipedia-corpus|English Wikipedia at 2,500M words]], so about 3.3 billion words in total, with lists, tables and headers stripped out of Wikipedia.

The corpus has to be [[document-level-corpus|kept at document level]], because long contiguous spans cannot be sampled from shuffled sentences. The paper names [[billion-word-benchmark|the Billion Word Benchmark]] as the kind of corpus it is deliberately not using.

[[training-steps-and-epochs|The budget multiplies out]]. Batches hold 256 sequences of up to 512 tokens, which is 128,000 tokens per step, and training runs for 1,000,000 steps. That is about 128 billion tokens seen, or roughly 40 passes over 3.3 billion words.

[[sequence-length-schedule|Length is scheduled rather than fixed]]: 90% of steps use sequences of 128 tokens, and only the last 10% use 512. Attention scores every pair of positions, so [[attention-quadratic-cost|quadrupling cost with doubled length]] is what makes short sequences worth it, and the final stretch is there to train the position rows near the end of the table.

[[combined-pretraining-loss|The training loss is just the sum]] of the mean [[masked-language-model|masked-LM]] likelihood and the mean next-sentence likelihood. This is the expensive half of the paper; everything after it costs about an hour at a time. [[theme-the-two-pre-training-tasks|The two objectives]] and [[etheme-the-pre-training-run|the run that trained them]] are covered in detail there.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Turning it into a task model
chapters.body:
Pre-training leaves one set of weights that has never seen a labeled example. [[fine-tuning-bert|Fine-tuning]] is what turns them into a model for entailment, or tagging, or span extraction.

The paper's answer is that only the ends change. [[task-specific-input-output-plugging|The task's texts are mapped onto the A and B slots]], and an output layer is attached to the right hidden vectors. A single-text task is handled as [[degenerate-text-pair|a pair whose second half is empty]]. [[fig-4|Four task shapes are drawn as four copies of one diagram]], differing only in what is packed in and which vectors an arrow leaves from.

One argument does real work here. Because a packed pair is encoded together with attention that may cross the [SEP] boundary, [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|self-attention already includes attention between the two texts in both directions]]. Systems that encode two texts separately have to add a module for that. The argument only holds because the attention is unmasked.

[[task-specific-output-layer|The task-specific part is one layer]]. For a sentence classification task it is [[c-vector-classification-head|a single matrix applied to $C$]]: [[eq-classification-loss|multiply $C$ by $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$, softmax, ordinary cross-entropy]]. With three labels and $H=768$, that is 2,304 new weights against 110 million pre-trained ones.

For extractive [[question-answering]] it is thinner still. [[span-prediction-head|The span head]] introduces [[start-and-end-vectors|two $H$-dimensional vectors, $S$ and $E$]]. [[eq-span-start-probability|The start distribution is a softmax of $S \cdot T_i$ over the passage tokens]], and $E$ gives the end distribution the same way.

Decoding is arithmetic. [[eq-span-score|A candidate span from $i$ to $j$ scores $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$]], and the prediction is the highest-scoring pair with $j \geq i$. The score is a sum of two independent terms, so nothing in the model looks at the span as a unit.

[[end-to-end-fine-tuning|Encoder and new layer are then trained together]] on the labeled data. [[fine-tuning-cost|The paper puts the cost at an hour at most on one Cloud TPU]], a few hours on a GPU. [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|The grid is small]] — batch size 16 or 32, learning rate 5e-5, 3e-5 or 2e-5, and 2, 3 or 4 epochs — and cheap fine-tuning is what makes running all of it and keeping the best on dev affordable. [[theme-adapting-to-a-task|Adapting the model]] and [[etheme-one-added-layer-per-task|the one layer each task adds]] go through every head.

chapters.title: Eleven tasks and the numbers
chapters.body:
[[eleven-task-evaluation|The evaluation]] is one pre-trained encoder fine-tuned eleven times. The count is eight scored GLUE tasks, SQuAD 1.1, SQuAD 2.0 and SWAG.

[[glue-benchmark|GLUE]] supplies the sentence and sentence-pair half, each task a linear layer on $C$. [[table-1|The scoreboard]] reports BERT_BASE at 79.6 average and BERT_LARGE at 82.1, against 75.1 for [[openai-gpt]]. Subtracting gives the 4.5 and 7.0 points the abstract quotes, and both rows also lead in every individual column, which is what makes the average hard to pin on one easy task. On [[mnli|MNLI]], the largest of them, the gain is 4.6 points.

Two things about how that table was built are stated by the authors. GLUE has nine tasks and eight are scored, because [[wnli|WNLI is dropped]] on the grounds that its construction is problematic and no system beats the majority-class floor on it; the caption says outright that the Average column therefore differs from the official [[glue-score|GLUE score]], which is 80.5 for BERT_LARGE against 72.8 for GPT. And fine-tuning BERT_LARGE was sometimes unstable on the small sets, so [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|several restarts were run and the best kept on dev]]. Each cell reports one number and no spread.

[[squad-v1-1|SQuAD 1.1]] is 100k crowdsourced questions whose answers are spans of a Wikipedia passage. [[table-2|The comparison]] gives a single BERT_LARGE 91.8 test F1 and a seven-model ensemble 93.2, against 91.7 for the best ensemble on the leaderboard — so +1.3 and +1.5, and the single model edges past the best ensemble it is measured against. Seven runs buy the last 1.4 F1.

That table carries an asterisk the paper supplies itself. Leaderboard entries may train on any public data, so BERT is first fine-tuned on [[triviaqa-augmentation|TriviaQA]]; removing it costs 0.1 to 0.4 F1, though those rows report dev scores only.

[[squad-v2-0|SQuAD 2.0]] allows questions with no answer in the passage. Abstention is handled without new machinery: [[cls-as-null-span|no-answer is scored as a span starting and ending at [CLS]]], compared against the best real span, with a threshold fitted on dev. [[table-3|The result]] is 83.1 test F1 against 78.0 for the best prior entry counted, a gap of 5.1 — and about 6.4 F1 below the 89.5 reported for humans.

[[swag-dataset|SWAG]] asks which of four continuations of a described situation is plausible. [[table-4|BERT_LARGE reaches 86.3%]], which is 27.1 points above the dataset authors' own ELMo-based baseline and 8.3 above GPT. It also sits above the 85.0 of a single human expert, but that human number comes from 100 samples, so it rests on far less than the model comparisons do. [[theme-the-eleven-tasks-and-the-scores|The tasks and their heads]] and [[etheme-the-eleven-task-scoreboard|how the scoreboard was assembled]] are both worth reading before quoting a figure.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: What each piece is worth, and what is not shown
chapters.body:
BERT is a bundle: bidirectional pre-training, a second sentence-pair objective, a lot of layers, a long run, an odd masking mixture. [[ablation-studies|The ablation programme]] takes pieces off one at a time.

[[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|Two cut-down models]] are pre-trained on the same data, with the same fine-tuning scheme and the same hyperparameters as BERT_BASE. [[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] keeps masked prediction and drops the sentence-pair task. [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]] goes further and masks attention to the left, which makes it an in-house stand-in for GPT that the authors control.

[[table-5|The numbers]] split cleanly. Dropping [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] moves QNLI from 88.4 to 84.9, and moves everything else under a point: MNLI 84.4 to 83.9, SQuAD 88.5 to 87.9, SST-2 92.7 to 92.6. Dropping bidirectionality costs far more, with MRPC falling from 86.5 to 77.5 and SQuAD F1 from 87.9 to 77.8.

The authors then try to repair the left-to-right model rather than leave it weak. [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|A randomly initialized BiLSTM on top]] lifts SQuAD F1 from 77.8 to 84.9, still well short, and pushes MRPC down from 77.5 to 75.7 and SST-2 from 92.1 to 91.6.

[[effect-of-model-size|The size ladder]] runs six separately pre-trained models from 3 layers to 24. [[table-6|Held-out masked-LM perplexity falls at every step, 5.84 down to 3.23]], and fine-tuned accuracy rises at every step, MNLI from 77.9 to 86.6. The point the paper draws is that the gains reach MRPC, which has 3,600 training examples. Its explanation — [[few-random-parameters-hypothesis|that adding very few random parameters lets a small task exploit a large representation]] — is offered as a hypothesis, not tested.

[[fig-5|Fine-tuning from successive checkpoints]] answers two more questions: MNLI is still gaining about a point between 500k and 1M steps, and the masked objective, behind at the earliest checkpoints, passes the left-to-right one early and stays ahead.

One ablation runs against the paper's own route. [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|BERT frozen as a feature extractor]] on [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]] reaches [[table-7|96.1 dev F1 with the top four layers concatenated, against 96.4 for fine-tuning]]. The 0.3 gap is small, though the frozen setting puts a two-layer BiLSTM back on top, so [[task-specific-architecture|task-specific architecture]] returns. And [[table-8|varying the masking mixture]] barely moves fine-tuned scores, while pre-training with [MASK] alone costs 0.9 F1 in that frozen setting. [[theme-taking-pieces-away|Each ablation]] is laid out in full there.

So what is established. Under matched data and fine-tuning, replacing a left-to-right objective with a masked one is worth about ten F1 on span extraction and does not come from scale or corpus. One encoder with one added layer matches or beats purpose-built architectures across eleven datasets, and the same encoder is nearly as good frozen.

What is not. NSP's contribution rests on a single column of one table, and no alternative sentence-pair objective is tried against it. The headline GLUE comparison with GPT is not matched on corpus or batch size, which the appendix says plainly, so the in-house left-to-right run is the cleaner of the two comparisons. The small-data columns involve keeping the best of several restarts, reported without spread. The human numbers on SWAG come from 100 samples, and on SQuAD 2.0 the model is still about six F1 short of people. Nothing here inspects what the representations actually encode, and [[single-task-vs-multi-task-fine-tuning|multi-task fine-tuning]] is raised only as a possibility. The conclusion the paper itself writes is narrower than its abstract: that these findings generalize to deep bidirectional architectures, letting one pre-trained model handle a broad set of tasks.

n-the-data-problem.title: The data you have and the data you want
n-the-data-problem.intro: The parent named the practice BERT inherits. This level supplies what it left out: the second source of transferable parameters the paper also reviews and then drops, the actual sizes of the labeled sets at issue, the specific objectives that trained each generation of pre-trained representation, and the reasons the paper gives for each of the two routes.

chapters.title: Where the training signal comes from
chapters.body:
The paper reviews two places to get parameters worth reusing, and builds on one of them.

One source is [[unlabeled-text|plain running text]]. An objective that predicts text from text needs no annotator, because the corpus supplies both the input and the answer. The size of the training set is then limited only by how much text you can collect.

The other source is a large labeled task. [[supervised-transfer-learning|Transfer from supervised data]] trains on one annotated dataset and reuses those weights somewhere else. The paper's examples are entailment corpora and machine translation. It also points at computer vision, where fine-tuning a model pre-trained on ImageNet had become a standard recipe.

Section 2.3 gives that second source two sentences and moves on. [[language-model-pre-training|Pre-training on unlabeled text]] gets the rest of the section.

The paper does not run the comparison, so the preference is stated rather than measured. The difference in available scale is large, though. A big annotated entailment corpus holds a few hundred thousand sentence pairs. A corpus of books holds hundreds of millions of words.

Be precise about what [[transfer-learning|transfer]] actually moves. Not examples — weights.

The end task never sees the unlabeled corpus. Whatever that corpus contributed has to be carried entirely in the numbers sitting in the pre-trained parameters, which then serve as the initialization for training on the labeled data.

That is also why the gain should be largest on [[low-resource-tasks|tasks with too little labeled data to train a deep model from scratch]]. On such a task, most of what the finished model knows cannot have come from its own training set. The [[downstream-task|labeled end task]] supplies the objective and the output format; the corpus supplied the starting point.

chapters.title: What the labeled task asks for
chapters.body:
The split into two shapes decides what can be attached to a pre-trained model, so make it concrete.

A [[sentence-level-tasks|sentence-level task]] emits one label for the whole input, and that input may be a single sentence or a pair of them. MNLI, the multi-genre [[natural-language-inference|entailment]] set, is a pair task with three labels: the second sentence is entailed by the first, contradicts it, or is neutral with respect to it. [[mnli|It ships 392,000 training pairs]]. [[rte|RTE]] asks nearly the same question in binary form and ships 2,500.

Both are entailment. One has over 150 times the training data of the other.

That range is the practical case for pre-training. A single method that has to work at both ends of it cannot count on the labeled set to teach the model English.

A [[token-level-tasks|token-level task]] emits an output at every position instead. [[named-entity-recognition|Marking names]] on [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003]] means assigning each token a tag from a small set of entity types. Extractive [[question-answering|question answering]] on [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD]] means picking two positions in the passage, a start and an end, that bracket the answer.

The mechanical consequence is the interface. A sentence-level head reads one vector that stands for the whole sequence. A token-level head reads the full sequence of per-position vectors and produces one output per position.

The paper's complaint about one-directional pre-training is graded along exactly this line. It calls the restriction sub-optimal for sentence-level tasks, and says it could be very harmful for token-level ones, since deciding whether a token begins an [[answer-span]] depends on text lying on both sides of it.

That is an argument at this stage, not a measurement. The measurement comes much later, in the ablations.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: One vector per word, then one per occurrence
chapters.body:
What pre-training handed downstream changed shape twice.

The first form was [[pre-trained-word-embeddings|a table of word vectors]] learned once on a large corpus and reused across tasks. [[word-embeddings|Those vectors]] were trained by objectives of two kinds. One was ordinary left-to-right language modelling: predict the next word, then keep the embedding table. The other discriminated correct words from incorrect ones given the surrounding context on both sides.

That second objective already read both directions. It still produced exactly one vector per word type, so both directions were compressed into a single row of numbers that could not vary from sentence to sentence.

The same idea was then pushed to coarser units. [[sentence-embeddings|Sentence and paragraph vectors]] were trained by ranking candidate next sentences, by generating the next sentence's words left-to-right from a representation of the previous one, or by objectives derived from denoising autoencoders.

Mark the next-sentence objective in passing. It is already in the field's toolkit here, applied to fixed sentence vectors.

The second change of shape is [[contextual-representations|the move to one vector per occurrence]]. The model reads the sentence and emits a vector at each position, so the same word form gets different vectors in different sentences and the vector can carry which reading is in play.

[[context2vec|One such model]] predicts a single word from both its left and its right context using [[lstm|LSTMs]]. The paper mentions it, calls it feature-based, and adds that it is not deeply bidirectional.

That last phrase is doing work. Both sides being used somewhere in a model is not the same as every layer conditioning on both sides, and that distinction is what the paper's objection turns on.

chapters.title: Freeze it, and build around it
chapters.body:
[[transfer-strategies|The paper sorts all of this prior work into two routes]], and the [[feature-based-approach|first]] treats the pre-trained model as a fixed feature extractor.

Concretely: run the frozen model over the input, take the vectors it produces, and feed them as extra inputs to a separate model that is trained from scratch on the labeled data.

[[elmo|ELMo]] is the paper's example. It trains a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]] and a [[right-to-left-language-model|right-to-left language model]], separately, and forms each token's contextual vector by concatenating the two directions' representations. Those vectors are then fed into an existing [[task-specific-architecture|architecture built by hand for the task]]. On that arrangement, ELMo advanced the state of the art on [[question-answering]], sentiment analysis and [[named-entity-recognition]].

The GLUE row for this system names the whole stack: BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn. The pre-trained part is one term in that name. The [[bilstm|BiLSTM]] and the attention layer are the task model, and they are where the design effort goes.

The paper gives two reasons why anyone would want this. First, not every task is easily represented by a [[transformer-encoder]], so some tasks need an architecture of their own regardless. Second, an expensive representation can be computed once over the training data, after which many cheaper models can be trained on top of it.

Neither reason is dismissed. Section 5.3 later runs BERT itself this way.

[[fig-3|The figure that lines up the three pre-training architectures]] draws ELMo's two directions as separate stacks, joined only at the top. That drawing is where the paper's objection starts, and the objection is the next chapter's.

chapters.title: Train the whole thing further
chapters.body:
The [[fine-tuning-approach|second route]] keeps almost nothing separate. Add a small output layer, then keep training every pre-trained parameter on the labeled data.

This route has a history of transferring steadily more. The earliest work in the direction pre-trained only the word embedding table from [[unlabeled-text]], and trained the rest of the network from scratch. Later work pre-trained whole sentence and document encoders, which produce contextual token vectors, and fine-tuned those.

The paper names the advantage plainly: few parameters need to be learned from scratch. [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|That is the stated design goal]] — adapting to a new task should add as few new weights as possible.

The pre-training objectives used on this route were left-to-right language modelling and autoencoder objectives.

[[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] is the paper's example here, and its closest point of comparison. GPT pre-trains a left-to-right Transformer language model on [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus]], 800 million words, then fine-tunes on each end task. The paper credits it with the previous state of the art on many of the [[sentence-level-tasks|sentence-level tasks]] in [[glue-benchmark|GLUE]], and attributes that at least partly to how few parameters start out random.

One detail of GPT's design matters later. Its separator and classifier tokens are introduced only at fine-tuning time, so pre-training never sees them.

[[bert|BERT]] places itself on this route deliberately. Appendix A.4 says many of BERT's design decisions were made to keep it as close to GPT as possible, so that the two could be compared with as little else differing between them.

That is the setup. Two routes, one shared kind of pre-training objective, and an objection to that objective still to come.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

n-only-one-side.title: Only one side of the sentence
n-only-one-side.intro: The parent stated the constraint and the paper's case against the obvious repair. This level goes down to the machinery: where in a Transformer the restriction actually lives, how strongly the paper claims it hurts and for which route, what prior work had managed on both sides, and how much of the argument is measured rather than asserted.

chapters.title: One triangle in the attention grid
chapters.body:
Inside a [[transformer-encoder|Transformer block]], [[self-attention]] has every position score every other position. For a sequence of $n$ tokens that is an $n \times n$ grid of scores $s_{ij}$, where $i$ is the position doing the reading and $j$ the position being read.

The left-only rule is applied to that grid and to nothing else. Before the softmax runs over $j$, every entry with $j > i$ is set to $-\infty$. Those entries come out of the softmax as zero weight, so position $i$'s output is a combination of positions $1$ through $i$ only.

Count what survives. Position 1 keeps one entry, position 2 keeps two, and so on up to position $n$, which keeps all $n$. That is $n(n+1)/2$ of the original $n^2$ — a little over half.

[[bidirectional-self-attention|Unmasked attention]] and [[constrained-self-attention|the masked version]] have the same weight matrices, the same shapes and the same forward code. What separates them is one boolean per pair of positions.

The objective is what puts the triangle there. A [[left-to-right-language-model]] is trained on $\prod_i p(x_i \mid x_{<i})$, and every position in the sequence is one of those predictions. All $n$ predictions are made in a single forward pass, which is only sound if position $i$'s stack is blind to its right at every layer.

So the mask is not an architectural preference. It is what an $n$-predictions-per-pass language model objective requires.

The naming in the literature marks exactly this line, as a footnote in Section 3 observes: the unmasked stack is usually called a Transformer encoder, and the left-context-only stack a decoder, since that one can generate text.

Nor can the triangle simply be dropped afterwards. Section 5.1 reports that removing the left-only constraint at fine-tuning time introduced a [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|pre-train/fine-tune mismatch]] that made downstream results worse, so [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|the paper's own left-to-right model]] keeps the mask downstream too. Removing it during pre-training instead is a different problem, since a token would then reach its own prediction — [[see-itself-problem|the "see itself" problem]].

chapters.title: Sub-optimal, or very harmful
chapters.body:
The introduction states the damage at two different strengths in one sentence. The restriction is called sub-optimal for [[sentence-level-tasks|sentence-level tasks]], and it could be very harmful for [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]] such as [[question-answering|question answering]]. The paper does not argue for the gap between those two verdicts.

A structural reading is available. A sentence-level task collapses the whole input to one label, and a left-only stack does have one position — the last — that has read everything. A token-level task reads out a vector per position, and [[final-hidden-vector-ti|the vector at position $i$]] is what the output layer sees.

Under the left-only mask that vector was built from $x_1 \ldots x_i$ and nothing else. For extractive question answering the model must mark an [[answer-span|answer span]] in a passage. A token near the front of the passage has to be judged as a plausible span start on the strength of the text before it, which is mostly the question.

The paper adds a second asymmetry, this one across [[transfer-strategies|the two transfer routes]]. It says the limitation bites hardest on fine-tuning approaches.

The reason is where the task model lives. On the [[feature-based-approach|feature-based route]] the frozen vectors are handed to a [[task-specific-architecture|separately built task model]], and that model may itself be bidirectional — a [[bilstm|BiLSTM]] over the features mixes left and right after the fact.

On the [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuning route]] the pre-trained network is the task network. There are [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|almost no new weights]] on top to do any repairing.

Whether the after-the-fact repair works at all is the question [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|the BiLSTM-on-top experiment]] is built to answer, and that comes later.

chapters.title: What both sides had already been tried for
chapters.body:
ELMo trains two models. One is a multi-layer [[lstm|LSTM]] running left to right; the other is the same thing running right to left, and each is trained with its own [[right-to-left-language-model|directional]] objective. Each token's [[contextual-representations|contextual representation]] is then the two directions' vectors joined end to end.

What matters is what each training loss could see. The left-to-right model's layer-two vector at position $i$ was computed with no right-side information at any depth, because no right-side state ever entered its forward pass. The join happens once, after both models are finished.

That is the operational content of [[shallow-concatenation|shallow]]. It is not about how good the features are; it is about how many layers of computation come after the two sides meet. In [[elmo|ELMo]] the answer is none.

[[context2vec]] moves the join earlier in one respect. Its objective predicts a single word from its left context and its right context together, using LSTMs, so both sides do enter one prediction. The paper's verdict is that it is still feature-based and, like ELMo, not deeply bidirectional: both sides are combined at one point, for one target word, rather than at every layer for every position.

So [[deep-bidirectionality|deep bidirectionality]] is a claim about placement. The two sides must meet inside the stack, with more layers of computation running on the mixed representation afterwards.

This whole line sits one step past [[pre-trained-word-embeddings|pre-trained word embeddings]], which give a word form the same vector wherever it appears. Contextual models vary the vector by sentence. Every system named here is in that second stage, and the disagreement is only about which parts of the sentence get to vary it.

chapters.title: The case against two models, weighed
chapters.body:
Take [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|the three reasons]] one at a time, since they are not the same kind of claim.

The cost reason is arithmetic. Two directional models of a given width are two full pre-training runs and two sets of parameters, against one run and one set for a model that reads both ways. It says nothing about which representation is better.

The [[question-answering|question-answering]] reason turns on input order. For SQuAD the question and the passage go into [[packed-question-passage-sequence|one packed sequence]], question first, passage second. A right-to-left model reads that sequence from the end, so it reaches the passage before it reaches the question.

Follow one passage token. Its right-to-left vector is built from the tokens to its right, which are the remainder of the passage and then the end of the sequence. The question is to its left, so the right-to-left half of that token's representation has never seen the question it is meant to answer.

The third reason is the one about quality. The paper says the concatenation is strictly less expressive than a deep bidirectional model, which can use both left and right context at every layer.

That one is asserted, not shown. [[table-5|The pre-training ablation]] holds data, input format and fine-tuning fixed and varies the objective, but the variants it runs are a bidirectional model without [[next-sentence-prediction]] and a left-to-right model. Nowhere in [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|that experiment]] is a separately trained left-to-right plus right-to-left pair concatenated and fine-tuned.

So the ELMo-style option is argued away rather than measured. It is the one competitor in [[theme-the-one-direction-problem|this part of the paper]] that never gets a number.

chapters.title: The picture, and what it does not control
chapters.body:
[[fig-3|The three-model figure]] is a connectivity diagram and makes a connectivity claim. Its caption also carries a second and unrelated axis: BERT and [[openai-gpt|GPT]] are fine-tuning approaches while ELMo is feature-based, which is a fact about how each is used downstream, not about arrows.

At this point in the paper that is all the picture establishes. It says what is being asserted; it measures nothing.

[[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison|Appendix A.4]] then lists what the diagram cannot show, and the list is not short. GPT pre-trains on [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus]] alone at 800M words, while BERT adds [[english-wikipedia-corpus|English Wikipedia]] for about 3.3B — roughly four times the text.

GPT introduces its separator and classifier tokens only at fine-tuning time. BERT learns [[cls-token|[CLS]]], [[sep-token|[SEP]]] and [[segment-embeddings|the A/B segment embeddings]] during pre-training, so they arrive downstream already trained.

Both run for 1M steps, but GPT's batch holds 32,000 words and BERT's holds 128,000. At equal step counts that is four times as many tokens seen. And GPT uses a single fine-tuning learning rate of 5e-5 everywhere, while BERT [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|picks one per task]] on the development set.

Against that, one thing is controlled deliberately. [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] is built at $L{=}12$, $H{=}768$, $A{=}12$ and 110M parameters, [[gpt-size-match|matched to GPT]] so that a score gap cannot be charged to capacity.

The matched size controls capacity and nothing on the list above. The paper states this itself, and points at the Section 5.1 ablations as its reply, since those vary the objective while holding the rest fixed. [[etheme-two-routes-one-direction|The two-route framing]] is what makes the comparison worth setting up this carefully.

n-one-stack-used-twice.title: One stack, used twice
n-one-stack-used-twice.intro: The chapter above gave the shape of the framework. This one supplies the parts: what physically crosses between the two steps, what the paper imports rather than describes, how a single mask accounts for the whole architectural difference from GPT, and where the two parameter counts come from.

chapters.title: What actually crosses between the steps
chapters.body:
[[bert-framework|The framework]] is easier to hold if you ask what physically moves from step one to step two.

What moves is a checkpoint: one file holding the weights of the entire encoder, produced once by pre-training on [[unlabeled-text]]. [[fig-1]] draws that crossing as dotted arrows, and every arrow lands on a matching block in the right-hand panel. Nothing is left behind — the embedding tables cross, and so does every layer of the stack.

The word "all" in "all of the parameters are fine-tuned" is doing real work here.

Once a [[downstream-task|task]] begins, those pre-trained weights keep moving under gradient descent, alongside the freshly initialized [[task-specific-output-layer]]. That is [[end-to-end-fine-tuning]]. It is what separates this route from the [[feature-based-approach]], where the pre-trained model is frozen and only its activations are handed onward.

So the weights a task *adds* are few — [[minimal-task-specific-parameters]] is the stated design goal. The weights a task *changes* are all of them.

That has a consequence the paper records without dwelling on it. [[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task]] means eleven tasks leave you with eleven complete copies of the network, each 110M or 340M parameters, differing from one another everywhere rather than only in a head. [[unified-architecture-across-tasks]] is a claim about shape, then, not about sharing weights at serving time.

The economics come out lopsided, which is the point of splitting the work in two. Pre-training each model took four days on a bank of Cloud TPUs. [[fine-tuning-cost]] is at most an hour on a single one, for any result in the paper.

The expensive step happens once. The cheap step happens eleven times.

chapters.title: The stack the paper declines to describe
chapters.body:
[[bert-model-architecture|The architecture section]] is unusually short, and it is worth being precise about what the citation to Vaswani et al. is carrying.

It carries a [[transformer-encoder]]: a stack of identical blocks, each pairing multi-head [[self-attention]] over the whole sequence with a position-wise feed-forward network, wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization. The paper names the tensor2tensor release as the implementation and points readers at a guide called "The Annotated Transformer" for the rest. Its justification is simply that Transformers have become common.

Two properties of that borrowed stack matter for everything that follows.

The first is that shape is preserved. $N$ token vectors go into a layer and $N$ vectors of the same width come out, one per position. Stacking more layers therefore changes nothing about the interface — the top of the stack still emits one vector per input token, written [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]].

The second is that this is the encoder half only. There is no decoder stack and no separate module for attending from one text to another. Whatever a task needs must be arranged inside that single sequence.

"Almost identical to the original" also has at least one documented exception, and the paper puts it in an appendix rather than here. The activation inside each block is [[gelu-activation|gelu]] rather than relu, following GPT.

One cost is inherited along with the design. Every layer scores every pair of positions, so [[attention-quadratic-cost|attention is quadratic in sequence length]] — doubling the input roughly quadruples the attention work. The paper cites exactly this to explain a choice in its [[pre-training-procedure]], where most steps run on short sequences and only the last stretch runs on long ones.

chapters.title: Same operation, different mask
chapters.body:
Take one attention head at one layer. Each position projects its incoming vector into a query, a key and a value. The query at position $i$ is dotted with the key at every position $j$, giving one score per pair. A softmax over those scores turns them into weights, and position $i$'s output is the weighted sum of the values.

A mask enters between the scoring and the softmax. It is not a module; it is a decision about which scores are allowed to survive, with the rest driven to $-\infty$ so their weights come out at zero.

[[bidirectional-self-attention]] is this operation with no mask at all: every $j$ is admitted, left of $i$ and right of $i$, at every layer. [[constrained-self-attention]] admits only $j \le i$. [[fig-3]] draws the difference as arrows, with [[openai-gpt|GPT's]] arrows running one way and [[elmo|ELMo's]] two one-way stacks meeting only at the top — [[shallow-concatenation]] rather than [[deep-bidirectionality]].

So the architectural change is a triangle of $-\infty$ that BERT does not add. It costs nothing to remove and buys no parameters.

Which raises the obvious question: if it is that cheap, why did anyone mask?

Because the mask is not there for the architecture's sake. It is there for the objective's. A [[left-to-right-language-model]] trains each position to predict the next token, and without the mask that token is already visible to the position predicting it — [[see-itself-problem|the model can see itself]] and the objective collapses to copying.

That is the real content of [[unidirectionality-constraint|the one-direction problem]]. Removing the mask is free; replacing the objective it protected is not, and [[masked-language-model|the next chapters]] are about what BERT trains on instead.

chapters.title: Where 110M and 340M come from
chapters.body:
[[model-size-notation|$L$, $H$ and $A$]] look like three independent dials, but they are tied together, and walking the count shows how.

Start with one block at hidden size [[hidden-size-h|$H$]]. Attention needs four $H \times H$ projection matrices — query, key, value, and the one that recombines the heads — for $4H^2$ weights. The feed-forward network goes out to $4H$ and back, since [[feed-forward-filter-size|the filter size is fixed at four times the hidden size]], for $H{\times}4H + 4H{\times}H = 8H^2$. One block is therefore about $12H^2$ weights.

For BERT_BASE, $H=768$, so $768^2 = 589{,}824$ and one block runs to roughly 7.1M. Twelve blocks give about 85M. The embedding table adds [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|30,000]] rows of width 768, another 23M, with [[position-embeddings|position]] and segment rows on top. Those two pieces land near 108M, which is the quoted 110M.

Run it again at $H=1024$. A block is about 12.6M, twenty-four of them about 302M, and the embedding table about 31M — roughly 333M against a quoted 340M. The paper never breaks the figure down, so the remainder is presumably biases, layer norms and rounding.

Notice what $A$ does not do. Twelve heads across 768 dimensions gives 64 dimensions per head; sixteen heads across 1024 gives 64 as well. The paper does not remark on it, but its two configurations widen the model by adding heads of a fixed size rather than by widening each head.

So [[bert-base-and-bert-large|the step from BASE to LARGE]] doubles depth, multiplies width by a third, and triples the parameter count. Whether that step pays off is settled later, on [[effect-of-model-size|a ladder of six sizes]].

chapters.title: A controlled comparison, and what it fails to control
chapters.body:
[[gpt-size-match|Building BERT_BASE at GPT's size]] sets up one clean inference. If the two score differently on the same benchmark, the gap is not capacity, because capacity was held equal on purpose. In [[table-1|the GLUE scoreboard]] the averages come out 79.6 against 75.1.

The paper does not leave that inference standing on its own, and the honest reading is in an appendix rather than in the results. [[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison|Appendix A.4]] lists four differences that the size match does nothing about.

GPT was pre-trained on [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus]] alone, 800M words. BERT was pre-trained on that plus [[english-wikipedia-corpus|English Wikipedia]], 2,500M more — over four times the text.

Both ran for one million updates, but GPT's batches held 32,000 words and BERT's held 128,000 ([[training-steps-and-epochs|128,000 tokens per batch]]). At equal step counts, BERT saw about four times as many tokens.

GPT introduced [[cls-token|its classifier token]] and [[sep-token|its separator]] only at fine-tuning time, so those embeddings started cold; BERT learned them during pre-training. And GPT used one fine-tuning learning rate everywhere, while BERT [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|searched a small grid per task]].

Four times the data, four times the tokens, warm special tokens, and a tuned learning rate. The matched parameter count controls one variable and leaves those.

The paper says as much, states its core argument as a claim about the two pre-training tasks and the bidirectionality they enable, and points to an in-house ablation instead: [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|a left-to-right model of its own]], trained on the same data with the same hyperparameters, [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|varying only the objective]]. That comparison is the stronger evidence. [[theme-one-architecture-two-stages|The architecture and its two stages]] end here; the objective is what the next chapters take up.

n-one-input-format.title: One input format for every task
n-one-input-format.intro: The parent named the parts of the format. This level walks what each part costs and what it rules out: how loose the word "sentence" really is, what WordPiece does to a word before the model sees it, how big each of the three embedding tables actually is, and why one of them puts a hard ceiling on sequence length.

chapters.title: What actually goes in the two slots
chapters.body:
The definition of [[sentence-as-arbitrary-span|a "sentence" as any contiguous span]] is not just terminological caution. Appendix A.2 says the two spans sampled for pre-training are "typically much longer than single sentences (but can be shorter also)". So slot A may hold a paragraph.

That has a consequence for the data. The spans have to be contiguous stretches of real text, which means the [[pre-training-data|pre-training corpus]] has to be [[document-level-corpus|kept as documents]] rather than as a shuffled bag of sentences.

Now the packing itself. [[sentence-pair-packing|Two spans go into one sequence]] as A and B, and [[sep-token|a [SEP] token]] closes each one. So a packed pair contains two [SEP] tokens, not one: one in the middle and one at the very end.

[[fig-2|The figure]] shows something easy to miss about the middle one. In `my dog is cute [SEP] he likes play ##ing [SEP]`, the first [SEP] is drawn carrying the A segment embedding. The separator belongs to the span it closes, not to the boundary between the two.

Both slots need not be filled. A single-text task uses [[degenerate-text-pair|a degenerate text-∅ pair]]: span A holds the text, span B is empty, and the sequence is just [[cls-token|[CLS]]], the text, and one [SEP].

Because the slots hold spans rather than sentences, lopsided pairs fit with no special handling. [[packed-question-passage-sequence|A question and the Wikipedia passage that answers it]] go in as A and B like any other pair, even though one is a clause and the other runs to hundreds of tokens. The only constraint binding the two together is a shared budget: [[max-sequence-length-512|their combined length]] has to fit inside one sequence.

chapters.title: Down to pieces the model already knows
chapters.body:
[[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]] is a fixed inventory of subword strings, learned from a corpus before BERT training begins. A word that is in the inventory becomes one token. A word that is not gets cut into pieces that are.

The figure's example shows the convention. "playing" appears as `play` and `##ing`, where the leading `##` marks a piece that continues a word rather than starting one. Any string can be reduced this way, in the worst case down to single characters, so the tokenizer never has to emit an unknown-word symbol.

[[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|The inventory holds 30,000 pieces]]. That one number does two separate jobs. It is the number of rows in the token embedding table on the way in, and it is the width of [[mlm-output-softmax|the output softmax used in pre-training]] — the layer that has to name which token was hidden.

The split has costs the paper mentions only in passing. Positions in the sequence are pieces, not words. [[masking-rate-15-percent|The 15% of positions chosen for masking]] are chosen after tokenization, with, in the paper's words, "no special consideration given to partial word pieces" — so a masked position can be `##ing` alone, with `play` left visible beside it.

Downstream the same seam reappears. A word split across pieces has no single vector, so for [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]] the paper feeds [[first-sub-token-classification|the first sub-token's vector]] to the tag classifier. That is a stated convention rather than a result; no comparison against averaging or taking the last piece is reported.

One thing to say plainly: WordPiece is cited here, not studied. The paper spends two sentences and a reference on it.

chapters.title: Three tables, one vector
chapters.body:
[[input-embedding-sum|The sum]] is possible because all three lookups return vectors of the same width. Each is a row in [[hidden-size-h|$\mathbb{R}^H$]], the width the encoder passes between layers, so the elementwise sum $E$ is in $\mathbb{R}^H$ as well.

Concatenation would not have that property. Three joined rows would make the input $3H$ wide, and the first block of [[transformer-encoder|the encoder]] would then need a different shape from every block above it. Summing keeps all the blocks identical, which is what lets the stack be described as the ordinary Transformer encoder with nothing bolted on.

The three tables are very different sizes. The token table has one row per vocabulary entry, so $30{,}000 \times H$. [[position-embeddings|The position table]] has one row per slot in the sequence, so $512 \times H$. [[segment-embeddings|The segment table]] has exactly two rows, A and B.

Put $H=768$, the [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] setting, and walk the arithmetic. The token table is $30{,}000 \times 768 \approx 23$ million parameters, roughly a fifth of BERT_BASE's 110 million. The position table is $512 \times 768 \approx 393{,}000$. The segment table is $2 \times 768 = 1{,}536$ numbers, and that is the whole apparatus for telling A from B.

The position table is the one that carries a consequence. Positions are learned rows, not a function of the index, so there is no row 513 to look up. 512 is a hard ceiling, not a soft one.

And a row only trains when sequences actually reach it. That is why [[sequence-length-schedule|the last 10% of pre-training steps]] switch to length-512 inputs, while the first 90% run at length 128 — [[attention-quadratic-cost|attention cost grows quadratically]] with length, so the long rows are paid for as late as possible.

chapters.title: Learned in pre-training, not bolted on at the end
chapters.body:
[CLS], [SEP] and the A/B embeddings are all part of the pre-training run. They are not notation introduced once a task shows up.

[[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison|Appendix A.4]] draws the contrast explicitly against [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]], the system the paper treats as its closest neighbour and [[gpt-size-match|deliberately matches in size]]. GPT has a separator token and a classifier token too, but introduces both only at fine-tuning time. BERT's arrive at fine-tuning with a million steps of training already behind them.

That is not free. The format has to be settled before pre-training begins, and any task whose shape does not fit one or two spans has to be bent into one or two spans.

The A/B slots also earn their keep inside pre-training. [[next-sentence-prediction|The second pre-training task]] asks whether span B genuinely followed span A, so [[isnext-notnext|its two labels]] are only expressible because the format already carries two marked halves.

A further design argument is attached to the packing, in Section 3.2. The common way to handle a text pair is to encode the two texts separately and then run [[bidirectional-cross-attention|cross attention]] between them. BERT concatenates instead, and the paper argues that [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|self-attention over the concatenation already does both jobs at once]]: every token of B attends to every token of A in the same operation that builds A's own representation.

Notice what kind of support that claim has. It is an argument from what self-attention computes, not a measurement. The ablations later in the paper isolate bidirectionality and the two pre-training tasks; they do not test packing against separate encoding, so this particular choice goes unmeasured while [[unified-architecture-across-tasks|the unified architecture]] it makes possible gets the credit.

chapters.title: Two vectors, and a caution attached to one
chapters.body:
[[final-hidden-vector-c|$C$]] sits at position 0 and [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]] at position $i$. Both are top-layer outputs, and both live in $\mathbb{R}^H$ — the same width as everything else in the stack.

The paper gives the [CLS] output its own letter rather than calling it $T_0$. The letter does work: it marks that this position is read as a summary of the whole sequence, not as one token's own representation.

Sharing the encoder's width matters more than it sounds. Because $C$ and $T_i$ are already $H$-dimensional, [[task-specific-output-layer|a task head]] can be a single matrix or a pair of vectors, and [[task-specific-input-output-plugging|adapting to a task]] reduces to choosing which positions to read from.

[[fig-4|The fine-tuning figure]] draws exactly that, as four copies of one diagram. Sentence-level heads attach to $C$. Token-level heads attach to the $T_i$. Nothing between the input and the top layer moves.

There is a caution the paper puts in a footnote, and it belongs here rather than later. [[c-not-a-sentence-representation|$C$ is not a meaningful sentence representation without fine-tuning]]. Before fine-tuning, the only gradient $C$ has ever received came from one binary decision about whether B followed A, so out of the box it is a vector shaped for that decision and nothing broader.

One more property of position 0 is worth flagging forward. Its output is not always read as a summary: [[cls-as-null-span|SQuAD 2.0 treats a span that starts and ends at [CLS] as "no answer"]], scoring abstention with the same [[start-and-end-vectors]] used on real tokens. The same slot serves as a summary in one task and as a candidate answer in another.

n-hiding-words.title: Masking, in procedure and in price
n-hiding-words.intro: The level above gave the objective and named its two costs. This one is the objective as a procedure: what the training-data generator actually does to a sequence, what each of the three branches of the recipe is separately there to prevent, and how much of that the paper's own ablations support.

chapters.title: What the generator does to a sequence
chapters.body:
Masking is the last step in building a training example, not the first.

[[training-sequence-generation|The generator samples two spans of text first]], assigns them the A and B slots, and caps their combined length at 512 tokens. Only then does it choose positions to hide. And it chooses them after [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece tokenization]] has already run.

The paper is explicit about what follows from that ordering. The rate is uniform over WordPiece positions, "with no special consideration given to partial word pieces". A rare word that has been split into three pieces is therefore three independent candidates.

The generator may select the middle piece and leave its two neighbours visible. So some targets are whole words restored from surrounding context, and some are fragments restored from the rest of their own word. The paper reports neither the proportion nor a comparison against masking whole words.

Now count the targets. [[masking-rate-15-percent|The 15% rate]] is applied per sequence, and [[sequence-length-schedule|90% of the steps run at length 128]] rather than 512. Fifteen percent of 128 is about 19 positions. Only in the last tenth of training does a sequence carry roughly 77.

The prediction head is thin. [[final-hidden-vector-ti|The top-layer vector at a selected position]] is projected through [[mlm-output-softmax|a softmax whose width is the vocabulary]] — [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|30,000 pieces]] — and scored by cross-entropy against the original token.

Positions that were not selected get no head and no loss term at all. That is [[denoising-autoencoder-contrast|the stated difference from a denoising autoencoder]] written as arithmetic: [[masked-language-model|the masked-LM term]] is a mean over about 19 positions, not over 128. [[combined-pretraining-loss|The full training loss]] is that mean added to the next-sentence term. Delete a word, ask for it back from both sides — [[cloze-task|the cloze procedure]] — run 19 times per sequence.

chapters.title: What each of the three branches is for
chapters.body:
The level above gave the split. The reasons are given one branch at a time, in Appendix A.1, and they are not the same reason.

Start with what a single branch would do. Suppose every selected position became [[mask-token|the [MASK] placeholder]]. Then the placeholder and the task would coincide exactly. A position holding an ordinary token would be a position the model is never asked about.

The paper's claim is that the model would learn precisely that. Its stated goal for [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|the mixture]] is that the encoder "does not know which words it will be asked to predict or which have been replaced by random words". Since [[bidirectional-self-attention|every position is visible to every other at every layer]], a representation the model has let go slack cannot be recovered further up.

Take the other two branches separately. Leaving 10% unchanged — [[mask-same-rnd-strategies|the SAME case]] — creates targets indistinguishable from ordinary input. The paper gives it a second, narrower purpose as well: to "bias the representation towards the actual observed word".

Replacing 10% with a random token does something sharper. It makes a visible token occasionally wrong. The model cannot read a position and take it at face value.

That branch carries a price the paper names and then waves through. For 1.5% of all tokens, the target asks for a word other than the one present in the input. The defence offered is the size of the number: random replacement "does not seem to harm the model's language understanding capability".

Seem is the paper's word. The only check on it is [[masking-procedure-ablation|the masking ablation]], and that ablation measures downstream scores rather than anything about the representations themselves.

Note also which side of the gap the whole apparatus works on. It changes pre-training so that pre-training looks a little more like what comes after. Nothing changes on [[fine-tuning-approach|the fine-tuning side]], where [MASK] still never appears, so [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|the mismatch]] is narrowed rather than closed.

chapters.title: Six runs that say the mixture barely matters
chapters.body:
Appendix C.2 pre-trains six models that differ in exactly one thing: what happens to a token once it has been selected. [[table-8|The table]] gives three [[dev-set-model-selection|Dev]] numbers for each.

Read the fine-tuned [[mnli|MNLI]] column first. The shipped 80/10/10 recipe scores 84.2. All-[MASK] scores 84.3. Eighty/twenty/zero scores 84.4, and eighty/zero/twenty scores 84.1.

Those four sit within 0.3 points of one another, and the highest is not the recipe the paper uses. The two rows that drop [MASK] entirely come in lower: 83.7 for 0/20/80, and 83.6 for all-random. The column spans 0.8 points end to end.

The paper's own word for this is "surprisingly robust". That is the honest reading. On a fine-tuned sentence-level task, the mixture is not what makes BERT work.

The one place the recipe earns something is the frozen setting. [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|Using BERT as a fixed feature extractor]] on [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]] means [[concat-last-four-layers|concatenating the top four layers]] and feeding [[frozen-feature-bilstm-classifier|a randomly initialised BiLSTM]] on top. There 80/10/10 scores 94.9 and all-[MASK] scores 94.0.

[[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|The stated reason]] is that a frozen model gets no chance to adjust. Fine-tuning lets the network unlearn a habit formed in pre-training. Freezing does not, and the habit in question is the one the mixture exists to prevent.

So the mechanism and the evidence line up here. Note the size of it, though: 0.9 F1, on one dataset, in one of three columns.

One more reading of the same table. The paper says that using RND alone "performs much worse than our strategy as well". Its numbers are 83.6 against 84.2 on MNLI, and 94.6 against 94.9 on frozen NER. Much is carrying more weight than the table gives it.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: The bill in gradient, and when it is paid off
chapters.body:
The second cost is easier to quantify than the first. Count the training signal per step.

A [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right model]] gets a target at every position of every sequence. At length 128 that is 128 predictions. [[masked-language-model|Masked LM]] gets about 19 from the same forward pass over the same batch — roughly one seventh of the supervision.

[[mlm-convergence-cost|The slower convergence]] follows from that, and the paper predicts it before measuring it.

[[fig-5|Figure 5]] is the measurement. It fine-tunes on MNLI from checkpoints taken at increasing pre-training step counts, and plots Dev accuracy against $k$. Two curves are drawn: BERT_BASE trained with masked LM, and [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|the same model trained left-to-right instead]].

At the earliest checkpoint the left-to-right curve is the higher one, near 79.4 against 78.6. The two cross somewhere around 100,000 steps. After that the masked curve stays above, finishing near 84.4 against 82.2 at a million.

The paper writes that MLM "begins to outperform the LTR model almost immediately". On its own figure that is right about almost. There is a window — about the first tenth of the run at this scale — in which the cheaper objective is ahead.

Read the axis carefully before drawing a cost conclusion from it. It counts steps, not hours. Both models are the same size and the same architecture, so a step costs about the same in each, but the paper charts no wall-clock or TPU time here. What the figure shows is efficiency per step.

The same figure answers a second question. [[effect-of-number-of-training-steps|Going from 500k steps to 1M]] buys almost a full point of MNLI accuracy, which is the paper's justification for [[training-steps-and-epochs|running the full million]]. The curve is close to flat over the last stretch. Nothing in it argues for going further.

What masking bought is [[deep-bidirectionality|a model whose every layer conditions on both sides]]. What it cost is a placeholder that never appears downstream, and six sevenths of the per-step signal. The ablations put a number on the second cost and struggle to put one on the first.
