n-the-second-task-and-the-run.title: The second task, and the run
n-the-second-task-and-the-run.intro: The level above stated the second objective and the training budget as facts. This one takes them apart: how a single training example is actually assembled and in what order, how hard the binary question really is, what the run cost in chips and days, how the length schedule reshapes it, and whether a million steps were needed.

chapters.title: How one example is assembled
chapters.body:
The two things being compared are called sentences throughout, but Appendix A.2 says plainly what they are: spans of text sampled from the corpus, typically much longer than a single sentence, though they can be shorter. Nothing enforces a sentence boundary. A and B are slot names, not linguistic units.

[[training-sequence-generation|Building one example]] happens in a fixed order, and the order matters.

First, two spans are sampled under one constraint: their combined length must not exceed [[max-sequence-length-512|512 tokens]]. The first span receives the A [[segment-embeddings|segment embedding]] and the second receives the B one, which is the only thing in the input marking which is which. The coin is flipped at this point — half the time B is the span that genuinely followed A, half the time it is a span drawn from elsewhere in the corpus.

Only then is masking applied. It runs after [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece tokenization]], at a [[masking-rate-15-percent|uniform 15%]] across the finished sequence, with, in the paper's words, no special consideration given to partial word pieces. So a rare word split into three pieces can lose its middle piece to a [[mask-token|mask placeholder]] while its two neighbours stay visible.

Masking does not respect the A/B boundary either. Appendix A.1's negative example is `[CLS] the man [MASK] to the store [SEP] penguin [MASK] are flight ##less birds [SEP]`, labelled NotNext — both spans are masked, the randomly drawn one included.

One forward pass over that sequence produces both the masked-position outputs and [[final-hidden-vector-c|the aggregate vector at the front]]. [[combined-pretraining-loss|The two losses]] are read off the same computation, not from two separate passes over two separate batches.

chapters.title: A question that is easy to get right
chapters.body:
The paper reports the finished model getting the binary question right 97-98% of the time. That figure appears in a footnote, and nothing in the paper is built on it.

It is worth being precise about what the rate measures. The labels are balanced, so chance is 50%, and the model's error rate is two to three points. That is a high score on a task whose negatives are made by [[isnext-notnext|drawing B from anywhere in the corpus]].

Consider what such a negative usually looks like. A span about a man walking to a store, followed by a span about flightless birds, shares almost no vocabulary and no subject matter. Telling that apart from a genuine continuation does not require any model of discourse order. Topical coherence is enough, most of the time.

So 97-98% is thin evidence that the objective teaches sentence relationships, and the paper does not use it that way. It points instead to Section 5.1, where [[no-nsp-ablation|a model pre-trained without the second task]] is compared under otherwise identical conditions; the largest single drop there is [[qnli|QNLI]] falling from 88.4 to 84.9. [[table-5|That table]] and [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|what it charges to each removed piece]] belong to a later chapter.

The footnote's caution follows from how $C$ was fitted. It was trained against this one label, so [[c-not-a-sentence-representation|it is not a general sentence embedding]].

That is tolerable only because of the transfer story. [[full-parameter-transfer-vs-sentence-embeddings|BERT hands every parameter downstream]] rather than a vector, so nothing ever consumes $C$ as pre-training left it — [[end-to-end-fine-tuning|fine-tuning rewrites it along with everything else]]. The objective has to shape the encoder. It does not have to leave behind a reusable vector.

chapters.title: The settings, the chips, the four days
chapters.body:
Appendix A.2 gives [[pretraining-optimizer-settings|the optimizer settings]] without arguing for any of them: Adam, learning rate $1\times10^{-4}$, $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, L2 weight decay $0.01$, dropout $0.1$ on all layers.

The learning rate is warmed up over the first 10,000 steps and then decayed linearly. Against a million steps, that warmup is the first 1% of the run.

One choice is marked as borrowed rather than justified: [[gelu-activation|gelu in place of relu]], following [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]]. No ablation is offered for it.

The hardware is stated for both sizes. [[bert-base-and-bert-large|The base model]] was trained on 4 [[cloud-tpu|Cloud TPUs]] in Pod configuration, 16 chips in total. The large model was trained on 16 Cloud TPUs, 64 chips.

Each pre-training took four days.

Notice what is held fixed across those two rows. The larger model got four times the chips and the same wall clock, so its extra capacity was paid for in hardware rather than in time.

Set that against [[fine-tuning-cost|what adapting the model costs]]: at most an hour on a single Cloud TPU, for any result in the paper. Four days on 64 chips, once, against an hour on four chips, per task.

That asymmetry is what makes the rest of the paper's method affordable. [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|A small grid searched per task]], and [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|several restarts]] where fine-tuning turned out unstable, all run off the one finished checkpoint.

The four days is the cost of one successful run. The paper does not say how many runs came before it, or what any of it cost in money.

chapters.title: Where the length schedule bites
chapters.body:
Start with the cost the schedule is answering to.

[[self-attention|Self-attention]] scores every pair of positions in the sequence. At length 128 that is $128^2 = 16{,}384$ pairs, per head, per layer. At length 512 it is $512^2 = 262{,}144$. Doubling the length twice multiplies the pair count by sixteen. The rest of [[transformer-encoder|the block]] grows only linearly with length, so [[attention-quadratic-cost|the quadratic term]] is what long sequences actually cost.

Hence [[sequence-length-schedule|the split]]: 900,000 steps at length 128, then 100,000 at length 512.

The stated reason for the second phase is [[position-embeddings|the position embeddings]]. These are a learned table with one row per position, 512 rows deep. Through the first 900,000 steps no input ever reaches position 128 or beyond, so rows 128 through 511 receive no gradient at all. They sit at their initial values for nine tenths of the run. The last tenth exists to train them.

There is an arithmetic loose end here. [[training-steps-and-epochs|The budget]] is quoted as 256 sequences times 512 tokens per batch — $131{,}072$, which the paper rounds to 128,000 — and the roughly 40 epochs follows from multiplying that by a million steps.

But 90% of those steps run at length 128, not 512.

The appendix does not say whether the batch was enlarged during the short phase to hold the token count steady. Read literally, the two statements do not both hold, and about 40 passes over the corpus is an upper bound rather than a count.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Whether a million steps was needed
chapters.body:
Appendix C.1 asks whether the run needed to be that long, and answers with a fine-tuning experiment rather than a pre-training loss curve.

The method is to take pre-training checkpoints at $k$ steps, fine-tune each one on [[mnli|MNLI]], and read accuracy on [[dev-set-model-selection|the development set]]. [[effect-of-number-of-training-steps|Plotting that against $k$]] gives [[fig-5]].

On the budget question, the reported answer is that the base model gains almost 1.0% MNLI accuracy at 1,000,000 steps compared with 500,000. The second half of the run — two more days on the same chips — buys about one point on one task.

Note the shape of that claim. The curve is still rising at a million steps, so what the figure supports is that the budget was not wasted, not that it was enough. And it is one task, at one model size, on a dev set.

The same figure answers a second question, this one about the objective rather than the length. Because [[masked-language-model|the masked LM]] makes a prediction at only 15% of positions, each step yields far fewer supervised targets than a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]], which predicts at every position.

[[mlm-convergence-cost|The reported answer]] has two halves. The masked model does converge slightly more slowly, and in absolute accuracy it passes [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|the left-to-right model]] almost immediately.

Fewer targets per step, then, but the paper reports that the slower convergence never surfaces as a deficit in downstream accuracy.

n-turning-it-into-a-task-model.title: Turning it into a task model
n-turning-it-into-a-task-model.intro: The parent gave the recipe: map the task's texts into the two slots, attach one layer, train everything. This level does the arithmetic inside that recipe — which vectors each task shape actually reads, how many fresh weights a head really adds, what the span decoder does and does not consider, and what running the whole hyperparameter grid costs.

chapters.title: What differs between the four panels
chapters.body:
[[fig-4|The four panels]] are labelled by task family, and reading them side by side is the quickest way to see what swapping the ends comes to.

Panel (a) is sentence pair classification, and it holds most of GLUE: [[mnli|MNLI]], QQP, QNLI, STS-B, MRPC, RTE, and SWAG as well. Panel (b) is single sentence classification, holding SST-2 and CoLA. Panel (c) is [[question-answering]], with [[packed-question-passage-sequence|the question in the A slot and the paragraph in B]]. Panel (d) is single sentence tagging.

One thing separates the top row from the bottom.

In (a) and (b), a single arrow leaves [[final-hidden-vector-c|$C$]], the vector above the classification token, and one label comes out for the whole input. These are the [[sentence-level-tasks|sequence-level tasks]]. In (c) and (d), an arrow leaves every [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]] instead, one per position. These are the [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]].

Panel (d) is worth making concrete, because "attach a layer to the token vectors" hides a decision. On [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003]] the paper formulates entity recognition as tagging and puts [[tagging-without-crf|a plain per-token classifier on top, with no CRF layer]], so tags are chosen independently of each other. And because [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]] splits rare words into pieces, there are more positions than words; [[first-sub-token-classification|the first piece's vector is what the tag classifier reads]].

One shape in panel (a) does not quite fit the head described for it. [[sts-b|STS-B]] is annotated with a graded similarity score from 1 to 5, not a class, and Section 4.1 still writes the GLUE head as a softmax with a cross-entropy loss. The paper does not say how the graded case is handled.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Why a pair needs nothing added
chapters.body:
The parent stated the argument. What the argument replaces is worth being concrete about.

[[prior-squad-systems|The pair models the paper contrasts itself with]] — it names Parikh et al. and Seo et al. — run in two stages. Each text is encoded on its own, by its own pass of a recurrent or convolutional stack. Then a separate module computes [[bidirectional-cross-attention|attention between the two encodings in both directions]]: every premise token attends over the hypothesis, and every hypothesis token attends back. Cross-attention is a component you build and bolt on.

BERT concatenates the two texts before the encoder runs at all. [[self-attention|Self-attention]] forms each position's next vector as a weighted sum over every position it may attend to. So a token in the question mixes in paragraph tokens at layer 1, and again at layer 2, and at all twelve or twenty-four layers. [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|The two stages collapse into one]].

Two conditions hold this up, and only one of them is stated in the section.

The first is that [[bidirectional-self-attention|attention is unmasked]]. Under [[constrained-self-attention|the left-context mask that [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] uses]], a token in text A can never attend to text B, since B lies entirely to its right. Attention would still cross the boundary, but in one direction only.

The second is that the model can tell the two texts apart after they are joined, which is what [[sep-token|the separator]] and [[segment-embeddings|the segment embeddings]] supply. Concatenation without those marks would hand the encoder one undifferentiated span.

Section 3.2 argues this rather than measuring it. It reports no experiment comparing a packed pair against a separately encoded one.

chapters.title: Counting the weights a task adds
chapters.body:
The paper states [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|as a design goal]] that adapting to a task should learn as few fresh weights as possible. The division is worth doing.

[[c-vector-classification-head|The GLUE head]] is one matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$ applied to $C$, followed by [[eq-classification-loss|a softmax and an ordinary cross-entropy loss]]. For MNLI, $K = 3$. With [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]], [[hidden-size-h|$H$]] is 768, so $W$ holds 2,304 numbers. With BERT_LARGE, $H$ is 1024 and $W$ holds 3,072.

Against 340 million pre-trained weights, that is roughly one fresh weight in every 110,000.

[[swag-dataset|SWAG]] adds less again. The task is to pick the plausible continuation of a described situation from four candidates — [[grounded-commonsense-inference|a judgment about everyday situations]] rather than logical entailment.

[[swag-multiple-choice-head|The head there is a single vector]], not a matrix. Each candidate continuation is packed with the context into its own sequence, so one example becomes four sequences. Each is encoded separately and yields its own $C$. The one learned vector is dotted with each of the four, and a softmax over those four scores picks the answer.

Sharing that vector across the candidates is what makes a single $H$-dimensional vector enough: 1,024 numbers for BERT_LARGE.

The shape has a cost the parameter count hides. A single training example is four forward passes through the encoder, not one.

[[task-specific-output-layer|The added layer]] therefore contributes almost no capacity. Whatever distinguishes entailment from paraphrase detection has to already be in the pre-trained weights; fine-tuning's job is to move them.

chapters.title: The span head, end to end
chapters.body:
[[span-prediction-head|The span head]] has a training objective the parent did not state. It is the sum of the log-likelihoods of the correct start position and the correct end position.

That is two separate classifications over positions. [[eq-span-start-probability|The start softmax]] runs over the tokens of the paragraph, and the end softmax runs over the same set. [[start-and-end-vectors|$S$ and $E$]] are trained by those two terms and by nothing else. No term in the loss ever looks at the pair together.

Decoding inherits the property. [[span-score-and-decoding|The search runs over every pair]] $(i, j)$ with $j \geq i$ and keeps the largest [[eq-span-score|$S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$]]. Nothing caps how long the predicted [[answer-span]] may be. Nothing rescores the tokens lying between $i$ and $j$.

[[squad-v2-0|SQuAD 2.0]] then allows [[unanswerable-questions|questions with no answer in the paragraph]], and the paper extends the head without adding a single parameter.

[[cls-as-null-span|Abstaining is treated as a span that starts and ends at the classification token]]. Both probability spaces are widened by that one position. [[null-span-score|The score of abstaining]] is $s_{null} = S \cdot C + E \cdot C$, formed from the same two vectors against $C$.

Prediction becomes a comparison. [[eq-null-answer-threshold|A real answer is emitted only when the best span beats $s_{null} + \tau$]], and [[tau-threshold|$\tau$]] is a scalar picked on [[dev-set-model-selection|the development set]] to maximise F1.

$\tau$ is worth naming for what it is. It is not a weight, and it is not trained by gradient descent. It is one number fitted after the fact, and it alone sets how readily the system declines to answer.

chapters.title: What a fine-tuning run actually costs
chapters.body:
[[end-to-end-fine-tuning|Training the encoder and the new layer together]] reuses most of the pre-training configuration. Dropout stays at 0.1 throughout. Three things vary: batch size, learning rate, number of epochs.

Walk the grid. Two batch sizes, three learning rates and three epoch counts make eighteen runs per task.

Now the price of one run. [[fine-tuning-cost|Every result in the paper]] is claimed reproducible in at most an hour on [[cloud-tpu|a single Cloud TPU]], and a footnote puts the SQuAD model at around thirty minutes there, reaching 91.0 Dev F1. Eighteen runs at that scale is well under a day on one machine.

That is what makes [[exhaustive-hyperparameter-search|running the entire grid and keeping the best on dev]] a reasonable thing to recommend rather than a luxury.

[[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|The stated grid]] is a recommendation, though, not a record of what was run. [[glue-fine-tuning-protocol|GLUE]] fixed batch size 32 and 3 epochs for every task and searched four learning rates, including 4e-5, which the appendix's list of three does not contain. SQuAD 2.0 used a batch size of 48, outside the stated pair.

Two caveats come from the authors themselves.

[[dataset-size-hyperparameter-sensitivity|Large datasets were far less sensitive to the choice]], around 100k labeled examples and up. The small sets are where the setting matters most, and they are also where the dev set used to choose it is smallest.

And [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|BERT_LARGE fine-tuning was sometimes unstable on small datasets]]. The remedy was several restarts from the same pre-trained checkpoint, differing only in data shuffling and in how the classifier layer was initialised, keeping whichever scored best on dev.

So a reported number can be the best of eighteen configurations and several restarts. The paper says as much openly. It yields [[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task|one selected model per task]], not one run per task.

n-eleven-tasks-and-the-numbers.title: Eleven tasks and the numbers
n-eleven-tasks-and-the-numbers.intro: The parent gave the totals. This level is what sits underneath them: what each column is actually scored on, which knobs were turned before a number was submitted, and how much of each headline margin you can read straight off the table.

chapters.title: Eight columns, and none of them the same thing
chapters.body:
Eight columns, and one head serving all of them. Whatever the GLUE task, fine-tuning adds a [[c-vector-classification-head]]: one weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$ applied to $C$, then a softmax and ordinary cross-entropy. Only $K$, the number of labels, changes from task to task.

What changes far more is what sits under each column.

Training-set size runs from 392k examples on the largest set down to 3.5k on [[mrpc]] and 2.5k on [[rte]]. That is a spread of more than a hundred to one, inside a single row.

The metric changes too, and the caption says so outright. [[qqp]] and MRPC are scored by [[f1-score]], because one class dominates both and plain accuracy would flatter a lazy classifier. [[sts-b]] is scored by Spearman rank correlation, because its label is a 1-to-5 similarity rating rather than a class. The rest — MNLI, [[qnli]], [[sst-2]], [[cola]] and RTE — are accuracy.

So the Average column in [[table-1]] is a mean over quantities that are not the same quantity.

Two more reading notes. MNLI carries two numbers split by a slash: matched, where the test genres also appear in training, and mismatched, where they do not. And the acceptability column sits far below every other column for every system in the table, so it has to be read on its own scale rather than against its neighbours.

The protocol behind the cells is thin. [[glue-fine-tuning-protocol]] fixes batch size at 32 and training at 3 epochs for every one of the eight tasks. The only knob turned per task is the Adam learning rate, chosen from 5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5 and 2e-5 on the [[dev-set-model-selection]] split.

One knob, eight tasks.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Two averages, and what a single cell hides
chapters.body:
The paper reports two different GLUE averages, and they are not the same number.

Table 1's Average column covers eight tasks and gives BERT_LARGE 82.1 against 75.1 for [[openai-gpt]]. Subtract and you get the 7.0. The official leaderboard aggregate, quoted in the running text, gives 80.5 against 72.8. Subtract those and you get 7.7 — which is the figure the abstract quotes.

Both are in the paper. They differ because one includes WNLI and one does not.

The exclusion has a stated floor behind it. Always predicting the most frequent label — the [[majority-class-baseline]] — scores 65.1 on WNLI, and the GLUE page notes that every submitted system has come in below that. The authors say they drop the set to be fair to OpenAI GPT, and that in their own submission they simply predicted the majority class.

Next, what one number per cell is hiding. [[fine-tuning-random-restarts]] means several runs from the same pre-trained checkpoint, differing only in data shuffling and classifier-layer initialisation, with the best kept on Dev. That selection bites hardest where the data is thinnest — RTE at 2.5k, MRPC at 3.5k.

Those are also the columns where BERT_LARGE's margin over BERT_BASE is widest, which the paper credits to [[effect-of-model-size]]. No spread is reported, so the two effects cannot be pulled apart from the table.

Then the search behind each cell. GLUE withholds test labels, and the [[glue-evaluation-server]] scores submissions; the paper says it made exactly one submission per model size. Everything else is therefore settled on Dev, where the small [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] grid makes [[exhaustive-hyperparameter-search]] affordable.

Every row is [[single-task-vs-multi-task-fine-tuning]] — one model per task. A footnote adds that multi-task training with MNLI gave substantial improvements on RTE, with no number attached.

All of these gaps are stated as [[absolute-improvement]], points of difference rather than relative gain. And because [[bert-base-and-bert-large]] sizes BASE to GPT deliberately ([[gpt-size-match]]), 79.6 against 75.1 is the row-to-row comparison the argument rests on.

chapters.title: SQuAD 1.1: from a dev number to a leaderboard row
chapters.body:
Fine-tuning for span extraction adds two vectors and nothing else.

Question and passage go in as a [[packed-question-passage-sequence]], the question tagged A and the passage tagged B. The [[span-prediction-head]] introduces [[start-and-end-vectors]] $S$ and $E$, each of dimension $H$. [[span-score-and-decoding]] scores a candidate running from $i$ to $j$ as $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, and predicts the highest-scoring pair with $j \geq i$. Training maximises the sum of the log-likelihoods of the correct start and the correct end.

Three epochs, learning rate 5e-5, batch size 32. A footnote reports that this run takes about 30 minutes on one Cloud TPU and reaches 91.0 Dev F1, which is [[fine-tuning-cost]] made concrete.

Two metrics run across the table, [[exact-match-and-f1]]. A prediction that catches the right words but runs one word long earns most of an F1 point and zero EM, which is why F1 sits above EM in every row.

Now the ladder. BERT_BASE reaches 88.5 Dev F1. BERT_LARGE reaches 90.9. Ensembling seven systems, built from different pre-training checkpoints and different fine-tuning seeds, adds 0.9 to give 91.8 Dev.

Those rows carry Dev only. The two submitted rows add [[triviaqa-augmentation]] and report Test: 91.8 single, 93.2 ensemble.

The comparison entry is nlnet's ensemble at 91.7 Test F1. So $93.2 - 91.7 = 1.5$, and that margin reads straight off the table.

The +1.3 for the single system does not fall out of the same subtraction — 91.8 against 91.7 is +0.1. What the table does show plainly is the sharper claim: one BERT scores above the best ensemble on the board.

Two conditions the paper states itself. Those top entries have no current public system descriptions and may train on any public data, which is [[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules]]. And the [[prior-squad-systems]] in the Published block are purpose-built reading-comprehension architectures with attention machinery between question and passage — replaced here by two vectors.

[[ensembling]] buys 1.4 Test F1 for seven times the fine-tuning.

chapters.title: Scoring the decision not to answer
chapters.body:
The extension to SQuAD 2.0 is one position and one scalar.

[[unanswerable-questions]] are given an [[answer-span]] whose start and end are both the [CLS] token. The probability space of [[eq-span-start-probability]] — the softmax over passage tokens — is widened to include that position. Abstaining becomes a candidate span like any other.

Scoring it needs no new weights. [[null-span-score]] is $s_{null} = S \cdot C + E \cdot C$: the same $S$ and $E$ as SQuAD 1.1, read against $C$ instead of against a passage token.

Against it stands the best real span, $\hat{s}_{i,j} = \max_{j \geq i} S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, which is [[eq-span-score]] unchanged.

The decision rule is [[eq-null-answer-threshold]]: answer only when $\hat{s}_{i,j} > s_{null} + \tau$.

That $\tau$ is the one genuinely new thing. [[tau-threshold]] is a single scalar, and it is not learned by gradient descent — it is swept on the development set to maximise F1. So the abstention policy is fitted on the same split the Dev column reports.

The run: 2 epochs, learning rate 5e-5, batch size 48, and no TriviaQA this time.

The numbers are 78.7 EM / 81.9 F1 on Dev and 80.0 / 83.1 on Test. Against MIR-MRC (F-Net) at 78.0 Test F1, $83.1 - 78.0 = 5.1$. The single model also leads the best Published ensemble by 8.2 F1.

Two limits sit on the same page. The Human row is 89.5 Test F1, leaving BERT 6.4 short. And the caption excludes any entry that already uses BERT as a component, so this is a filtered board rather than the whole one.

One thing the table cannot tell you: no run with a separate answerability classifier is reported alongside it. The 83.1 shows the reuse is sufficient, not that it beats the alternative.

chapters.title: Four sequences, one vector
chapters.body:
Multiple choice does not fit the classification head, so the input format is bent instead of the head.

Each SWAG example becomes four sequences rather than one. The context sentence goes in the A slot and one candidate continuation goes in the B slot, using the same [[sentence-pair-packing]] as everything else. The encoder is then run once per candidate.

The scoring is [[swag-multiple-choice-head]]: a single learned vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^H$, dotted with each sequence's [[final-hidden-vector-c]] to give four scores, normalised by a softmax over the four.

The task-specific parameters are therefore one vector — not a matrix, as on GLUE, and not two vectors, as on SQuAD. The cost moves elsewhere: four forward passes per example instead of one.

Three epochs, learning rate 2e-5, batch size 16.

What the task asks is [[grounded-commonsense-inference]] — which continuation of a described situation is plausible, judged by everyday knowledge rather than by entailment. With four choices, guessing lands near 25%.

The ladder in Table 4 is worth walking, because it separates two things. ESIM is a sentence-pair [[natural-language-inference]] model built on a [[bilstm]]. Fed static GloVe vectors, which give every occurrence of a word the same vector, it scores 52.7 on Test. Fed [[elmo]]'s context-sensitive vectors instead — same task model, different word representations — it scores 59.2. A fine-tuned left-to-right Transformer then reaches 78.0, and BERT_LARGE 86.3.

$86.3 - 59.2 = 27.1$. $86.3 - 78.0 = 8.3$.

The larger figure is measured against a baseline the SWAG authors built for their own paper, so the 8.3 over GPT is the more informative of the two.

The human rows read 85.0 for one expert and 88.0 for five annotations combined. BERT sits above the first and below the second. The dagger says both come from 100 samples, thin enough that a point or two either way carries little.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

n-what-each-piece-is-worth.title: What each piece is worth, and what is not shown
n-what-each-piece-is-worth.intro: The chapter above gave the results. This level gives the designs that produce them: what each run holds fixed, which column moves under which removal, and where a score the paper calls competitive is in fact behind. It also separates the one controlled comparison from the one that gets quoted.

chapters.title: Two removals, and what makes them chargeable
chapters.body:
An ablation only charges a cost to one piece if nothing else moved. [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|The pre-training ablation]] holds three things fixed against BERT_BASE: the [[pre-training-data|pre-training corpus]], the fine-tuning scheme, and the fine-tuning hyperparameters. The rest of [[pre-training-procedure|the pre-training recipe]] is the one already described.

[[no-nsp-ablation|The first cut-down run]] removes one loss term. Masked prediction stays; the [[next-sentence-prediction|sentence-pair task]] and its [[isnext-notnext|IsNext/NotNext label]] go. Nothing about the input format changes, so the model still packs two spans and still reads them through [CLS].

[[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|The second]] changes the objective itself. Instead of predicting masked positions it predicts the next token, which means [[constrained-self-attention|masking attention so that a position may attend only to positions at or before it]].

One detail decides how far this run can be pushed. The left-only constraint is kept at fine-tuning as well.

Lifting it there would let the fine-tuned model attend rightwards when no pre-training step ever did. The paper names that a [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|pre-train / fine-tune mismatch]] and reports that it degraded downstream scores. So the run stays left-only end to end, which is what lets it stand in for [[openai-gpt|GPT]] rather than for a half-converted BERT.

Now the NSP column. In [[table-5|the ablation table]], removing NSP costs 3.5 points on [[qnli|QNLI]], 88.4 down to 84.9. On [[mrpc|MRPC]] it costs 0.2, 86.7 down to 86.5.

That is one Dev column from one pre-training run, with no spread reported. No alternative sentence-pair objective is put up against it.

chapters.title: Where one-sided context actually costs
chapters.body:
The comparison that measures bidirectionality is not BERT_BASE against the left-to-right run, because those two differ in two ways at once. The pair to read is [[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] against LTR & No [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]], since neither has the sentence-pair loss.

Column by column the gap is uneven. [[mnli|MNLI]] falls 1.8, from 83.9 to 82.1. QNLI falls 0.6. [[sst-2|SST-2]] falls 0.5. MRPC falls 9.0, from 86.5 to 77.5. [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD]] F1 falls 10.1, from 87.9 to 77.8.

So the two removals do not hurt the same tasks. NSP's largest loss was QNLI, where losing [[deep-bidirectionality|both-sided context]] costs almost nothing.

For SQuAD the paper says the reason is plain. The [[span-prediction-head|start and end head]] scores each passage token by reading [[final-hidden-vector-ti|that token's final vector]]. Under left-only attention that vector was built from the tokens up to it and no further, so a token cannot know what follows it.

[[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|The repair]] adds a randomly initialised [[bilstm|BiLSTM]] above the encoder during fine-tuning. Right-side context arrives, but only in that one layer; the twelve layers below still never mixed it. SQuAD F1 goes 77.8 to 84.9, a gain of 7.1, and stays 3.0 under No NSP.

It costs elsewhere. MRPC drops to 75.7 and SST-2 to 91.6, while MNLI does not move. The added weights start random and are trained only on the task's own labels, and MRPC supplies 3,600 of them.

The paper also names the option it declined: [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|separate left-to-right and right-to-left models]], concatenated, as [[elmo|ELMo]] does. Its objections are cost, that a right-to-left model cannot condition an answer on the question before it, and that [[shallow-concatenation|joining two one-sided models at the top]] is weaker than conditioning both ways at every layer.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Two ladders: more layers, more steps
chapters.body:
[[effect-of-model-size|The size ablation]] pre-trains six models from scratch and fine-tunes each. [[table-6|The table]] lists them in [[model-size-notation|the L/H/A shorthand]]: layers, [[hidden-size-h|hidden size]], attention heads.

Read down it. At L=3, H=768, A=12 the held-out [[masked-language-model|masked-LM]] perplexity is 5.84, with Dev accuracies of 77.9 on MNLI, 79.8 on MRPC and 88.4 on SST-2. At L=6 with A=3, perplexity is 5.24 and the accuracies are 80.6, 82.2, 90.7. The next row keeps L=6 and H=768 and raises heads alone from 3 to 12: perplexity 4.68, accuracies 81.9, 84.8, 91.3.

That pair is worth pausing on. Depth and width are held, and head count by itself moves every number.

The ladder then runs through [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] at 3.99 / 84.4 / 86.7 / 92.9, a 12-layer model at H=1024 (3.54), and BERT_LARGE at 3.23 / 86.6 / 87.8 / 93.7.

These accuracies are averages over five [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|random restarts]], not a best-of. That is a stricter protocol than the headline GLUE table uses.

The claim rests on the small column. MRPC rises 8 points across the ladder on 3,600 examples. [[prior-scaling-evidence|Earlier evidence was mixed]] — two to four bi-LM layers gave no clear gain, and a hidden size of 600 beat 200 while 1,000 beat neither — and both prior results were feature-based. [[few-random-parameters-hypothesis|The explanation offered]] is written as a hypothesis, and no run here varies the count of fresh parameters to test it.

[[effect-of-number-of-training-steps|The second ladder]] fine-tunes from checkpoints taken at $k$ pre-training steps. [[fig-5|The curve]] gives almost 1.0 more MNLI accuracy at 1M steps than at 500k.

It also settles a worry about [[mlm-convergence-cost|masked prediction converging more slowly]]: only [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% of positions]] are predicted per batch, against every position for a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right model]]. The masked line does start behind, then passes before 100k steps and ends about two points ahead.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Freezing the encoder, and what that setting exposes
chapters.body:
[[feature-based-approach-with-bert|The one ablation that questions fine-tuning itself]] freezes the encoder. Its testbed is [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]], with case-preserving WordPiece and the maximal document context the data supplies.

The fine-tuned setup is deliberately thin. NER is cast as tagging [[tagging-without-crf|with no conditional random field over the tag sequence]], and where WordPiece splits a word, [[first-sub-token-classification|the first piece's vector]] is what the tag classifier reads.

The frozen setup cannot stay that thin. Activations are extracted with no parameter updated, then fed to [[frozen-feature-bilstm-classifier|a randomly initialised two-layer, 768-dimensional BiLSTM]] before the classifier.

[[layer-selection-ablation|Which layers to tap]] becomes its own ladder in [[table-7|the NER table]], in Dev F1. Embeddings alone give 91.0. The last hidden layer gives 94.9 and the second-to-last gives 95.6, so the top layer is the worse of the two. A weighted sum of the last four gives 95.9, [[concat-last-four-layers|concatenating the last four]] gives 96.1, and a weighted sum of all twelve gives 95.5.

Fine-tuned BERT_BASE gives 96.4, which is where the 0.3 comes from. Both sides of that gap are Dev numbers; the frozen rows carry no Test score at all. On Test, fine-tuned BERT_LARGE reaches 92.8 against 93.1 for the strongest prior system listed, so "competitively" is doing real work as [[state-of-the-art|the comparison word]].

[[masking-procedure-ablation|The masking ablation]] borrows this frozen setting for its sharpest column. Six pre-training runs vary the probabilities of [[mask-same-rnd-strategies|MASK, SAME and RND]]. Across all six, [[table-8|the fine-tuned scores]] sit between 83.6 and 84.4 on MNLI and between 94.8 and 95.4 on NER.

Frozen, [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|the 80/10/10 mixture]] scores 94.9 and a MASK-only run scores 94.0. [[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|The stated reason]] is that a fine-tuned model can adapt to inputs containing no [MASK] and a frozen one cannot.

That 0.9 F1 is the entire case for the mixture. On fine-tuned MNLI, an 80/20/0 run scores 84.4, above 80/10/10's 84.2.

chapters.title: What the ablations license, and what they don't
chapters.body:
Two comparisons in the paper point at the same conclusion, and only one of them is controlled.

[[table-1|The GLUE scoreboard]] puts BERT_LARGE 7.0 average points above GPT. Appendix A.4 lists four ways those runs differ beyond the objective. GPT trains on BooksCorpus alone, 800M words, where BERT adds Wikipedia for 3,300M. Both run 1M steps, but GPT's batch holds 32,000 words and BERT's holds 128,000. GPT introduces [SEP] and [CLS] only at fine-tuning, while BERT learns them, and the A/B [[segment-embeddings|segment embeddings]], during pre-training. GPT fine-tunes every task at 5e-5; BERT picks a rate per task on Dev.

So the 7.0 is not chargeable to bidirectionality. The in-house left-to-right run is, and its number is smaller: against BERT_BASE it gives up 2.3 on MNLI and 10.7 SQuAD F1.

Reporting is not uniform across the four ablation tables either. Tables 6 and 7 average five restarts. Tables 5 and 8 state no such protocol, and every ablation figure is Dev.

That matters more because the headline results already lean on selection. On the smaller GLUE sets, fine-tuning BERT_LARGE was unstable, so several restarts were run and [[dev-set-model-selection|the best was chosen on Dev]], reported without spread.

Some questions the programme never asks. Nothing removes a layer or a head from a trained model to see what it had encoded. [[single-task-vs-multi-task-fine-tuning|Multi-task fine-tuning]] appears once, as a possibility. The human baselines are thin: [[swag-dataset|SWAG]]'s comes from 100 samples, and on [[squad-v2-0|SQuAD 2.0]] the gap to people is still open.

[[theme-taking-pieces-away|Each experiment is laid out in full here]].

What [[ablation-studies|the programme]] does establish is narrow and real. With corpus and fine-tuning held fixed, the objective alone is worth about ten F1 on span extraction. The conclusion the paper writes claims that, and stops there.

n-the-data-problem--word-types-to-occurr.title: One vector per word, then one per occurrence
n-the-data-problem--word-types-to-occurr.intro: The parent named two shapes of pre-trained representation and the objectives behind them. This level walks each objective as a training procedure — what is predicted from what, what gets kept afterwards, and what the resulting data structure can and cannot do.

chapters.title: Two objectives, one table
chapters.body:
The paper spends two sentences here and gives one citation per objective. Both produce the same artifact, a table of [[word-embeddings]]. Both run on [[unlabeled-text]] alone, which is what puts them under [[language-model-pre-training]] at all.

The first objective is ordinary next-word prediction. A [[left-to-right-language-model]] is fitted to put probability on each token given the tokens before it. Such a model needs an embedding table at its input, because words have to enter the network as vectors somehow.

That table is not what the model was built for. It falls out of fitting it.

So the recipe for [[pre-trained-word-embeddings]] is: fit the language model on a large corpus, discard everything above the input layer, keep the table.

The second objective does not model the probability of text at all. It sets up a discrimination. Here is a position with words to its left and words to its right; here is the word that actually stood there; here are words that did not. The model is trained to tell them apart.

The paper does not say why that form was attractive, but the mechanical difference is worth naming. Predicting the next word properly needs a softmax normalised over the whole vocabulary, so every training step touches the output vector of every word in it. Scoring one true word against a few sampled false ones touches only those few.

Either way the same object reaches a [[downstream-task]]: a table someone else trained, dropped in where a randomly initialised embedding table would have gone.

The evidence offered for that being worth doing is one clause and one citation — significant improvements over embeddings learned from scratch. No numbers are given at this point in the paper. The motivation is the ordinary [[transfer-learning]] one, that [[low-resource-tasks]] cannot afford to learn what words mean from their own labels.

chapters.title: What a lookup table can and cannot do
chapters.body:
Both objectives end in the same data structure. It is a matrix with one row per vocabulary entry: $|V|$ rows of $d$ numbers each. For a vocabulary of 100,000 words and $d = 300$ that is 30 million numbers, though the paper quotes no such figures here.

The row for a word is selected by the word's spelling and by nothing else.

Now take the second objective's use of both directions seriously. Its training signal genuinely came from both sides of the target position. But every occurrence of *bank* anywhere in the corpus contributed its gradient to the same row. The river occurrences and the money occurrences pulled on the same $d$ numbers.

What settles out is one compromise vector. It could not be otherwise, because the structure has no slot for a second reading and no input at use time that would select between readings.

The consequence lands downstream. Whatever [[task-specific-architecture]] consumes these vectors has to recover which sense is in play from its own layers, trained on its own labeled data — the scarce resource. That bites hardest on [[token-level-tasks]], where a decision is needed at every position: a tagger doing [[named-entity-recognition]], a span finder doing [[question-answering]]. It also bites on [[sentence-level-tasks]], just less visibly.

Mark the general shape of the argument, because the paper returns to it. An objective can read both directions without the representation it leaves behind being bidirectional in any usable sense.

That gap — between where both directions were consulted and where both directions are available — is the same gap the [[unidirectionality-constraint]] argument later opens between [[shallow-concatenation]] and [[deep-bidirectionality]].

chapters.title: The same trick on bigger units
chapters.body:
[[sentence-embeddings]] and paragraph vectors apply the identical move one level up: a single fixed-size vector standing for a whole span, pre-trained once and reused. The paper lists three objective families that were used to train them.

The first ranks candidates. Given a sentence, its true successor is presented alongside sentences pulled from elsewhere, and the representation is trained so the true one scores highest. This is the wrong-word discrimination of the previous chapter with sentences as the negatives instead of words.

The second generates. A sentence is encoded to a vector, and the next sentence's words are then decoded from that vector, left to right. The pressure is reconstruction: the vector has to carry enough about the first sentence for a decoder to write the second.

The third denoises. A sentence is corrupted, and the model is trained to produce the original back. What the representation must hold is whatever the corrupted input has to be compressed to on the way through.

All three transfer the same kind of object — one vector per span, fixed once trained.

Two of these come back later in the paper, so note where. The ranking objective is the one BERT's [[next-sentence-prediction]] task is said to be closely related to, with its true/random pairing labeled [[isnext-notnext]]; the stated difference is not the objective but what moves downstream ([[full-parameter-transfer-vs-sentence-embeddings]]). The denoising family gets a [[denoising-autoencoder-contrast]], because [[masked-language-model]] predicts only the corrupted positions rather than reconstructing the whole input.

And a caution the paper puts in a footnote: the pre-trained [[cls-token]] vector is [[c-not-a-sentence-representation]] on its own. Whatever BERT is offering, it is not a better fixed sentence vector.

chapters.title: When the vector is computed instead of stored
chapters.body:
[[contextual-representations]] change what is actually stored. There is no longer a matrix indexed by word identity. There are the weights of an encoder.

Getting a vector for a word is no longer a lookup. You run the encoder over the sentence the word appears in and read the output at that position. The paper's later notation for such a per-position output is [[final-hidden-vector-ti]], the top-layer vector at position $i$.

Different vectors for the same word form now need no special machinery. The same string in two sentences goes through two different computations, because the encoder's other inputs differ.

The costs are real and worth stating plainly. A lookup is one memory read; this is a forward pass over the whole sequence, paid every time, at training and at use. With [[lstm]] encoders it is a sequential scan, so the vector at one end of the sentence only reflects the other end after the scan has traversed everything between.

What gets distributed changes too. Shipping embeddings meant shipping a file of numbers that anyone could index. Shipping a contextual model means shipping weights that the recipient has to execute.

And because a whole trained network is now sitting there rather than a matrix, the [[transfer-strategies]] question becomes live for the first time. The network can be frozen and read off as features ([[feature-based-approach]]), or its weights can be trained further on the labeled task while [[minimal-task-specific-parameters]] are added on top ([[fine-tuning-approach]]).

Those two routes are the subject of the chapters after this one.

chapters.title: Both sides, one word at a time
chapters.body:
[[context2vec]] is the paper's one worked example in this line: a model trained to predict a single word from both its left and its right context, using recurrent encoders.

The mechanism is a hole. Pick a target position. Run one recurrent pass over the words to its left, and another over the words to its right. Join the two resulting states into one context vector, and predict the missing word from that.

It is fill-in-the-blank — the same shape as the [[cloze-task]] the paper names later when describing its own objective.

The two passes are not two independently trained models joined at the end; there is no separate [[right-to-left-language-model]] here, only a rightward-reading half of one task. What matters is the other half of the phrase: *a single word*.

The context assembled to predict the target is built specifically to exclude the target. That exclusion is not tidiness. It is the only thing keeping the task from being trivial, because a representation at the target position that depended on the target would let the model read the answer off its own input.

The paper states this later as the [[see-itself-problem]], the reason standard conditional language models can only be trained in one direction.

So context2vec buys both directions by leaving one position out per prediction. What it offers is a representation of a hole's surroundings.

That is what "not deeply bidirectional" points at. The two directions meet once, at the join, near the top. A stack in which every layer already mixes both sides would give every position, at every depth, a representation that had seen both — which is what [[self-attention]] makes cheap to arrange, and what [[bidirectional-self-attention]] names.

n-only-one-side--the-picture-and-its-con.title: The picture, and what it does not control
n-only-one-side--the-picture-and-its-con.intro: Underneath the figure's arrows and the appendix's four bullets there are numbers, and the numbers change how large each difference is. This level walks the three panels one at a time, then puts arithmetic behind each item on the list, and closes on what the paper's own reply to that list gives up.

chapters.title: Three panels, two axes
chapters.body:
The figure is three stacks of boxes with arrows drawn between them. Each panel asserts which positions are allowed to feed which.

In [[fig-3]]'s first panel, arrows enter a position from its left neighbours and from its right neighbours, and they do so in every row of the stack. That is [[bidirectional-self-attention]] drawn as wiring.

The middle panel has arrows running one way only. This is [[constrained-self-attention]] — the same operation as the first panel, with the part of the attention pattern that would look rightward blanked out before the softmax.

The third panel is not one stack but two. A left-to-right [[lstm]] tower and a right-to-left tower stand side by side, and a line joins them only at the very top. That drawing is [[shallow-concatenation]]: the two directions are trained apart and meet once, at the output.

So the same claim is made three times over, and only the first panel satisfies it. [[deep-bidirectionality]] is a property of where the arrows are, not of how many directions appear somewhere in the diagram.

The caption then adds a sentence that the arrows have nothing to do with. It sorts the three models by [[transfer-strategies]], which is about what happens downstream: BERT and [[openai-gpt]] are [[fine-tuning-approach]]es, while [[elmo]] is a [[feature-based-approach]].

Read as two axes, the three panels are two independent binary splits, and BERT is the only model on the favourable side of both. It shares the downstream route with GPT, and shares access to text on both sides — in some form — with ELMo.

Neither axis implies the other. Nothing in ELMo's arrows requires freezing it, and nothing in GPT's requires fine-tuning it.

What no panel carries is a number. There is no corpus size in the picture, no step count, and no parameter count.

chapters.title: Four times the text, at the same number of passes
chapters.body:
Take the corpus first. GPT's [[pre-training-data]] is [[bookscorpus]] and nothing else, at 800M words. BERT adds [[english-wikipedia-corpus]] at 2,500M, for 3,300M in total, which is about 4.1 times as much text.

One property of the added text is not a size at all. Wikipedia is kept as running text with lists, tables and headers dropped, and the paper insists on a [[document-level-corpus]] so that long contiguous spans exist to be sampled.

Now the batch. Appendix A.2 gives BERT's as 256 sequences of 512 tokens, so $256 \times 512 = 128{,}000$ tokens per step. GPT's is quoted at 32,000 words per step. Both runs last 1,000,000 steps.

Multiply out. BERT's run touches $10^6 \times 128{,}000 \approx 1.28 \times 10^{11}$ tokens, and dividing by a 3.3-billion-word corpus gives about 39 passes — the "approximately 40 epochs" stated as [[training-steps-and-epochs]]. Do the same for GPT: $10^6 \times 32{,}000 = 3.2 \times 10^{10}$ over 800M words is also about 40.

So the two runs make roughly the same number of passes over their own data. The four-times factor is four times as much distinct text, not four times the repetition of the same text.

Units make this approximate rather than exact. The appendix counts GPT's batch in words and BERT's in [[wordpiece-tokenization]] pieces, and one word can become several pieces.

There is also a wrinkle inside BERT's own figure. The [[sequence-length-schedule]] runs 90% of steps at length 128 and only the last 10% at [[max-sequence-length-512]], because [[attention-quadratic-cost]] makes long sequences disproportionately expensive.

If the batch held 256 sequences throughout, the short phase would carry 32,000 tokens per step rather than 128,000, and the whole run would come to roughly twelve passes rather than forty. The stated batch and the stated epoch count reconcile only if the number of sequences rises while the length is small. The paper does not say which it did.

What it does say is the wall time: four days per run, BERT_BASE on 16 [[cloud-tpu]] chips and BERT_LARGE on 64.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Tokens that arrive with a history
chapters.body:
GPT introduces its separator and classifier tokens at fine-tuning time. Their embeddings are therefore initialised at random when the task starts, and every gradient they ever see comes from that task's labeled examples — sometimes only a few thousand of them.

In BERT the same pieces are load-bearing from the first step. Every pre-training sequence is built by [[sentence-pair-packing]]: two spans are drawn, the first marked A and the second B, with [[sep-token]] between them and another closing the sequence.

[[segment-embeddings]] are added to every token to say which span it belongs to. They are one of the three rows in [[fig-2]]'s [[input-embedding-sum]], beside the token embedding and the [[position-embeddings]], so they collect gradient on every token of every step rather than on a subset.

[[cls-token]] gets its training from the second objective. [[next-sentence-prediction]] reads [[final-hidden-vector-c]], the final vector at the [CLS] position, and classifies [[isnext-notnext]]. The paper reports the finished model at 97-98% on that binary decision.

Here the appendix's list becomes awkward. The trained [CLS] and segment embeddings are not an incidental extra; they are what NSP and the [[input-representation]] produce as a by-product.

NSP is one of the two pre-training tasks the paper is arguing for. So this item cannot be subtracted from the comparison without subtracting part of the claim under test.

Against that, the paper limits what the pre-trained tokens are worth. A footnote says C is [[c-not-a-sentence-representation]] without fine-tuning.

Arriving trained is therefore not the same as arriving usable. The claim is that the downstream model starts from vectors that have already been given a job, not that those vectors are already an answer.

chapters.title: One learning rate against eighteen runs
chapters.body:
[[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] in Appendix A.3 is a grid: batch size in {16, 32}, Adam learning rate in {5e-5, 3e-5, 2e-5}, and epochs in {2, 3, 4}. That is $2 \times 3 \times 3 = 18$ configurations per task.

The paper runs all of them. [[exhaustive-hyperparameter-search]] is affordable because of [[fine-tuning-cost]]: every result reproduces in about an hour on a single TPU, and the SQuAD model in roughly thirty minutes. The winner is chosen on the [[dev-set-model-selection]] split.

For [[glue-benchmark]] the protocol is narrower than the appendix's grid. [[glue-fine-tuning-protocol]] fixes batch 32 and 3 epochs for every task and varies only the learning rate, picked on Dev from 5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5 and 2e-5. Section 4.1 names four rates there where Appendix A.3's general range lists three.

GPT's single 5e-5 is itself a member of that grid. What the appendix reports as a difference is a search, then, not a different setting.

Where a search of this shape pays is something the authors state directly. [[dataset-size-hyperparameter-sensitivity]]: sets of 100k+ labeled examples were far less sensitive to the choice than small sets were.

The small sets are [[rte]] at about 2.5k examples, [[mrpc]] at 3,600, and [[cola]] at 8.5k. Those are exactly the columns where a per-task rate could move a score that a reader would otherwise charge to bidirectionality.

[[fine-tuning-random-restarts]] compounds this for BERT_LARGE, whose fine-tuning was sometimes unstable on the small sets. Several runs start from the same pre-trained checkpoint with different data shuffling and classifier initialisation, and the best on Dev is kept.

All of that selection happens on Dev, and the reported GLUE numbers come back from the evaluation server. The advantage is in how many attempts were made, not in which split was scored.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: What the matched size buys, and the reply
chapters.body:
[[model-size-notation]] is the paper's shorthand: $L$ blocks, hidden size $H$, and $A$ attention heads. [[bert-base-and-bert-large]] fixes two points on that grid — $L{=}12$, $H{=}768$, $A{=}12$ at 110M parameters, and $L{=}24$, $H{=}1024$, $A{=}16$ at 340M.

A footnote pins the one remaining width. The [[feed-forward-filter-size]] inside each block is $4H$, so 3072 when [[hidden-size-h]] is 768 and 4096 when it is 1024. Nothing about the configuration is left free once $L$, $H$ and $A$ are chosen.

[[gpt-size-match]] is a claim about the first of those two points. The paper says BERT_BASE was chosen to have the same model size as GPT, and Section 4.1 goes further, calling the two nearly identical in architecture apart from the attention masking. What the paper never prints anywhere is GPT's own parameter count, so the equality is asserted rather than shown.

The comparison this licenses is row against row. In [[table-1]] BERT_BASE averages 79.6 to GPT's 75.1, the 4.5 points Section 4.1 quotes, and on the official GLUE leaderboard BERT_LARGE reaches 80.5 against GPT's 72.8.

Which brings the list back. Matched capacity rules out one explanation of that gap and leaves the corpus, the pre-trained tokens, the batch and the tuning exactly where they were.

The appendix's answer is [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks]]. It trains [[no-nsp-ablation]] and [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation]] on the paper's own data, input format, fine-tuning scheme and hyperparameters, so all four items become shared rather than merely acknowledged.

Only the objective then changes — [[masked-language-model]] against a [[left-to-right-language-model]] — and the left-only constraint is held at fine-tuning too, to avoid a [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch]].

The price is that the controlled comparison is no longer against GPT. It is against a left-to-right model the authors built themselves, on their larger corpus and their input format. [[table-5]] holds those numbers.

So the paper ends up with two comparisons, and neither one is both against the real system and controlled.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

n-one-stack-used-twice--the-stack-not-de.title: Inside one block
n-one-stack-used-twice--the-stack-not-de.intro: The level above established that the block is borrowed and that it preserves shape. This one opens a single block and walks it in order — the head split, the scoring step, the per-position network, the wrapper, and the one substitution — marking at each step which number BERT actually chooses and which it takes from the citation.

chapters.title: Twelve heads of sixty-four
chapters.body:
A block of the [[transformer-encoder]] begins with [[self-attention]], and [[model-size-notation]] hands that sublayer exactly one number: $A$, the count of attention heads. Twelve in the smaller configuration, sixteen in the larger.

Here is what that number splits.

Each position arrives at the block holding a single vector of width $H$ ([[hidden-size-h]]). At the bottom of the stack that vector is [[input-embedding-sum|$E$]]; at the top it is [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]]. Three learned matrices turn a position's vector into three others: a query, a key, and a value.

Multi-head means those projections do not run at full width. The output is divided $A$ ways.

BERT's paper does not state the per-head width. The implementation it cites splits the model width evenly among the heads, which makes the arithmetic short. With $H=768$ and $A=12$, each head gets $768/12 = 64$ dimensions. With $H=1024$ and $A=16$, each head gets $1024/16 = 64$. The per-head width is 64 in both configurations — a coincidence the paper never remarks on, because it follows from the two settings it happens to list.

So for a sequence of $N$ [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]] tokens, one head holds $N$ queries, $N$ keys and $N$ values, each 64 wide. Each head then runs the whole attention operation on its own: its own scores, its own softmax, its own weighted sum. It emits $N$ vectors of width 64.

The $A$ heads' outputs are concatenated back to width $H$ and passed through one further learned matrix.

Note what the split does not buy. Twelve heads of 64 carry the same total projection width as one head of 768. The saving is not in compute. The heads buy the layer several separate attention patterns over the same positions instead of one.

[[bert-model-architecture]] fixes $A$, and nothing else about this sublayer.

chapters.title: Every pair, at every layer
chapters.body:
Now the operation a head runs, and where the cost shows up.

A head scores position $i$ against position $j$ by taking the dot product of $i$'s query with $j$'s key. That single number is divided by the square root of the head width — $\sqrt{64} = 8$ — which the cited work introduces to stop scores growing with dimension. A softmax over all $j$ turns position $i$'s row of scores into weights that sum to one. Position $i$'s output is those weights applied to the value vectors.

Count what that requires. For $N$ positions there are $N$ queries and $N$ keys, so the scoring step fills an $N \times N$ matrix, every entry a separate dot product. One such matrix per head, per layer.

This is [[attention-quadratic-cost]], and the arithmetic is worth walking rather than stating. At $N=128$ one head's score matrix holds $128 \times 128 = 16{,}384$ entries. At $N=512$ it holds $512 \times 512 = 262{,}144$. Four times the input, sixteen times the scores.

The paper cites exactly this. Appendix A.2, describing the [[pre-training-procedure]], says longer sequences are disproportionately expensive because attention is quadratic to the sequence length — and then acts on it. Ninety per cent of pre-training steps run at length 128, and only the final ten per cent at 512: the [[sequence-length-schedule]]. Sequences are assembled under a cap of 512 tokens ([[max-sequence-length-512]]) by [[training-sequence-generation]].

The stated purpose of that last stretch is narrow. It is to learn the [[position-embeddings]] for slots 129 through 512, which receive no gradient at all while training runs short.

The saving itself is asserted, not measured. [[training-steps-and-epochs|One million steps]] took four days on the [[cloud-tpu]] hardware reported, and no run at full length throughout is offered beside it.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: The sublayer that touches one position
chapters.body:
Attention is the only place in the block where information crosses between positions. The second sublayer does the opposite.

It takes each position's vector alone and pushes it through two learned matrices with a nonlinearity between them. The first widens $H$ to an inner width. The second brings it back to $H$. Nothing from any other position enters.

Footnote 3 sets that inner width: [[feed-forward-filter-size|four times $H$]], in all cases. Work it out — $4 \times 768 = 3072$ for the smaller configuration, $4 \times 1024 = 4096$ for the larger. The footnote states the ratio. It gives no argument for it, and the paper compares it against nothing.

"Position-wise" means the same pair of matrices is used at every position. It is one small network applied $N$ times in parallel, not $N$ different networks.

That puts most of a block's weight in the sublayer that does no mixing. Attention's four matrices are $H \times H$, so $4H^2$ parameters. The feed-forward pair is $H \times 4H$ twice, so $8H^2$. Twice as much matrix sits in the per-position transform as in the attention that connects positions.

One consequence surfaces much later in the paper. Because this sublayer never merges positions, a layer's output stays one vector per input token — which is what makes it meaningful to tap [[layer-selection-ablation|intermediate layers]] as features at all, and to [[concat-last-four-layers|join four of them]] per token.

The same property lets one stack serve [[token-level-tasks]] and [[sentence-level-tasks]] from a single forward pass. The per-token vectors survive to the top, and the [[cls-token]] position rides along beside them.

The nonlinearity in the middle is the one piece BERT replaces. That comes last.

chapters.title: What the addition forces
chapters.body:
Neither sublayer is used on its own. Each is wrapped.

The wrapper adds a sublayer's output back to that sublayer's input, then normalizes the sum — the original describes it as $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$. BERT's paper does not restate the arrangement. It names the tensor2tensor release and stops.

The addition is what forces the shape. For $x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ to be defined at all, the sublayer must hand back exactly the width it was given. That is why attention concatenates its heads back to $H$ instead of leaving twelve strips of 64, and why the feed-forward network has to climb to $4H$ and come back down. Preserved shape is not a design decision laid on top of the block. It is a precondition for the residual addition to be well formed.

The normalization runs across the $H$ features at one position. It pools nothing across the batch and nothing across positions, so like the feed-forward network it moves no information between tokens.

Two sublayers, two wrappers, so each block holds two residual additions. At $L=24$ that is forty-eight of them stacked, each offering the gradient a route past its sublayer rather than only through it — the difficulty that gating was introduced to handle in the [[lstm]], arising here along depth rather than along length.

Dropout sits at 0.1 on all layers, stated once in [[pretraining-optimizer-settings]] among the optimizer numbers.

The wrapper is also what makes $L$ a free knob. Every block consumes and returns the same object, so blocks compose without any interface changing. That is the property [[fig-1]] leans on when it draws one encoder used in two phases, and the property behind the claim of a [[unified-architecture-across-tasks]]. The [[final-hidden-vector-c|[CLS] vector]] read off the top is the same kind of object as the input fed in at the bottom.

chapters.title: gelu, and the size of the specification
chapters.body:
The nonlinearity between the feed-forward network's two matrices is [[gelu-activation]], not relu.

Where the paper says so is itself informative. Not in the architecture section. It appears in Appendix A.2, mid-list among optimizer settings, between the dropout rate and the training loss.

What the substitution changes: relu is a hard gate, passing $x$ when $x$ is positive and emitting zero otherwise. gelu multiplies $x$ by the probability that a draw from a standard normal falls below $x$. For large positive $x$ that probability approaches one and the function approaches $x$. For large negative $x$ it approaches zero. In between it is smooth, and small negative inputs are attenuated rather than cut.

The justification is one clause: following [[openai-gpt]]. No ablation against relu appears anywhere in the paper, and no measurement of what the swap is worth.

That is the whole architectural specification. $L$, $H$, $A$, a feed-forward width of $4H$, gelu, dropout 0.1, and the choice of attention mask. Two settings of those numbers are reported ([[bert-base-and-bert-large]]). Everything else in the block is a citation, a library name and a link to a guide.

How much of it is tested is quick to state. The ablations vary the pre-training objective — [[table-5]] removes [[masked-language-model|the masked objective]] and the next-sentence task — and separately vary model size. No experiment in the paper varies a block's internals. The BERT-versus-GPT differences listed in [[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison]] concern corpora, batch size, special tokens and learning rates; not one of the four is architectural.

So "almost identical to the original" stands on the authors' word, with a single exception they flag themselves.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

n-one-input-format--three-tables-one-vec.title: Three tables, one vector
n-one-input-format--three-tables-one-vec.intro: The level above gave the three shapes and walked the parameter counts at $H=768$. This one sets those counts against the rest of the model at both sizes, turns the case against concatenation into algebra rather than shape-matching, and follows the position table into the pre-training schedule, where the price of its longest rows can actually be counted.

chapters.title: A fifth of one model, a tenth of the other
chapters.body:
The row count of the token table comes from [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]], the subword scheme the input is tokenized with, and the paper fixes that inventory at [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|30,000 entries]]. That number does not move between model sizes. A larger BERT reads exactly the same set of pieces as a smaller one.

What moves is the width of each row, which is [[hidden-size-h|$H$]]. So the table is $30{,}000 \times 768 = 23{,}040{,}000$ parameters at the base width, and $30{,}000 \times 1024 = 30{,}720{,}000$ at the large one.

To see what that is a share of, count a block of [[transformer-encoder|the encoder]]. Self-attention holds four $H \times H$ projections — query, key, value, and the output projection — which is $4H^2$. The position-wise feed-forward layer holds two matrices of shape $H \times 4H$, since a footnote sets the filter size to $4H$, which is $8H^2$ more. Call it $12H^2$ per block.

At $H=768$ that is $589{,}824 \times 12 \approx 7.08$M per block, and twelve blocks give about $85$M. Add the $23.4$M held in all three tables and the total is roughly $108$M, against the $110$M reported for [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]]; the gap is biases, layer norms and the output heads.

At $H=1024$ a block is $1{,}048{,}576 \times 12 \approx 12.58$M, and twenty-four of them give about $302$M. With $31.2$M of tables that is $333$M against a reported $340$M.

So the tables are about 21% of BERT_BASE and about 9% of BERT_LARGE. Rows grow linearly in $H$; blocks grow with $H^2$, and the larger model has twice as many.

The 30,000 returns at the far end of the network, as the width of [[mlm-output-softmax|the masked-LM output softmax]].

chapters.title: Two rows, and what they are asked to carry
chapters.body:
[[segment-embeddings|The segment table]] is the smallest parameter block in the model that has a job of its own. Two rows at $H=768$ is 1,536 numbers; at $H=1024$ it is 2,048.

Assignment happens when the training sequence is built, not inside the model. Two spans are sampled, the first is given the A row and the second the B row, and the row is added at every position in its span. [[fig-2]] draws the boundary cases: the leading [[cls-token|[CLS]]] and the [[sep-token|[SEP]]] that closes the first span carry A, and the [SEP] that closes the sequence carries B.

Those two rows are what [[next-sentence-prediction|the next-sentence objective]] needs. Asking whether B genuinely followed A is only answerable if the model can tell which tokens are which.

The evidence for how much work the rows do is thin, though. The paper says it distinguishes the two spans in two ways — the separator token and the learned row — and reports no run that removes only the row. [[table-5]] ablates the next-sentence objective, not the embedding. Whether a model could recover the A/B split from separator positions alone is not tested here.

Downstream the same two rows are reused rather than replaced. Extractive [[question-answering]] tags the question A and the passage B in [[packed-question-passage-sequence|one packed sequence]]. Single-text tasks use [[degenerate-text-pair|a pair whose second half is empty]], which puts every token in A and leaves the B row without gradient for the whole fine-tuning run.

And [[sentence-as-arbitrary-span|A and B are spans]], not linguistic sentences, so the two rows are marking "first chunk" and "second chunk" and nothing finer.

chapters.title: Concatenation would not buy anything either
chapters.body:
The shape argument against concatenation has an algebraic version that is stronger, and it is worth doing because it says the choice costs nothing rather than merely being convenient.

Suppose the three lookups were stacked into one $3H$ vector, $2{,}304$ wide at the base setting, and then projected back to $H$ so the blocks above could stay identical. That projection is a $2{,}304 \times 768$ matrix, about $1.77$M parameters.

Now split it. A matrix $W$ applied to a stacked triple decomposes into three blocks, $W[a;b;c] = W_1 a + W_2 b + W_3 c$, each $W_i$ acting on one lookup alone. Each lookup is a row of a table that is trained from scratch. So $W_i$ applied to a table row is a function the table can simply learn to output directly.

Concatenate-then-project therefore spans the same set of input maps as [[input-embedding-sum|the plain sum]], while carrying $1.77$M parameters that have nothing to compute.

The argument depends on the tables being free. If one of them were fixed — frozen [[word-embeddings|pre-trained word vectors]], or positions given by a formula — a projection would have something to do that the table could not absorb.

The stack's shape is the other half of it. Every block reads a width-$H$ vector and writes one back, since [[self-attention]] and the feed-forward both preserve that width, so the input has to arrive at $H$ for [[bert-model-architecture|the architecture]] to be the ordinary encoder the paper claims it is.

What the sum gives up is separability. After the addition the first layer sees one vector, with no marked slot saying which part was position and which was token. The paper does not argue that this is harmless. It reports that [[final-hidden-vector-ti|the top-layer vectors]] work on eleven tasks, and that is the whole of the evidence offered.

chapters.title: There is no row 513
chapters.body:
[[position-embeddings|The position table]] is indexed by slot: row 0 for the first token of the sequence, row 511 for the 512th. Lookup, not computation.

The original Transformer defines position as a fixed function of the index, sinusoids that can be evaluated at any integer, so an input longer than anything seen in training still has a defined encoding. BERT's rows are parameters instead. There is no expression to evaluate at index 512, and no trained row to fetch.

So the ceiling is where the model stops rather than where it starts to degrade.

It is also tighter than 512 words. The count is in WordPiece pieces, and rare words are split into several, so a passage of $n$ words occupies more than $n$ slots. The classification token and both separators take three slots of their own, leaving about 509 for content in a packed pair.

The cap is enforced when the data is made. Two spans are sampled so that their combined length stays within the budget, which is one reason [[pre-training-data|the corpus]] is kept as [[document-level-corpus|whole documents]] rather than shuffled sentences: long contiguous stretches have to exist before long sequences can be sampled from them.

At the other end, [[fine-tuning-bert|fine-tuning]] inherits the same ceiling and the paper says less about it. For [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD]], a question and a passage share one sequence, and [[span-prediction-head|the start/end head]] scores only positions that exist in that sequence. An [[answer-span|answer span]] lying past the budget has no position to be predicted at.

The paper reports no procedure for inputs that overflow — no truncation rule, no sliding window. The ceiling is stated for pre-training sequence generation and left implicit everywhere else.

chapters.title: Paying for the long rows late
chapters.body:
Split the million steps of [[pre-training-procedure|pre-training]] the way [[sequence-length-schedule|the schedule]] does. Rows 0 through 127 receive gradient in all 1,000,000 steps. Rows 128 through 511 receive gradient in the final 100,000 only, a tenth as much exposure for three quarters of the table.

What that tenth saves can be counted from the paper's own numbers. Per block, per sequence, the matrix work is about $n \times 12H^2$ multiply-adds, linear in length $n$, while the pairwise part of [[attention-quadratic-cost|attention]] is about $2n^2H$. At $n=128$ and $H=768$ that is $906$M against $25$M. At $n=512$ it is $3.62$G against $403$M.

Total per block: $4.03$G against $931$M, a ratio near $4.3$. Four of that four-and-a-bit is simply four times as many tokens.

So the quadratic surcharge at this width comes to roughly 8% per token, not the sixteenfold factor the word "quadratic" suggests on its own. The stored score matrices do grow sixteenfold, which is a memory cost rather than an arithmetic one, and the surcharge keeps growing with length. The paper does not break the cost down this way; it says only that longer sequences are disproportionately expensive.

One piece of bookkeeping does not reconcile. [[training-steps-and-epochs|The quoted batch]] is $256 \times 512 = 131{,}072$ tokens, and a million such steps is about 40 passes over the 3.3 billion word corpus. But 900,000 steps at length 128 hold $32{,}768$ tokens each, giving $29.5$B, plus $13.1$B from the long phase — about 43 billion tokens, nearer 13 passes than 40. Whether the batch grows in sequences during the short phase is not stated.

No ablation isolates the schedule. [[fig-5]] shows accuracy still climbing at a million steps, but that curve does not separate steps from lengths.
