n-turning-it-into-a-task-model--the-span.title: The span head, end to end
n-turning-it-into-a-task-model--the-span.intro: The parent gave the objective and the decoding rule. This level follows one question through the head in order: how the example becomes a single sequence, what the two softmaxes are computed over and where their gradients go, what an additive score can and cannot rank, and what the abstention rule needs bolted on top of it.

chapters.title: One sequence, before any head
chapters.body:
Before either vector is used, one training example has to become one sequence of tokens.

[[squad-v1-1]] supplies a question and a Wikipedia paragraph, and the target is [[answer-span]]: a contiguous stretch of that paragraph, identified by where it starts and where it ends. The [[packed-question-passage-sequence]] puts both texts into a single input. [[cls-token]] goes first, then the question's tokens, then [[sep-token]], then the paragraph, then a closing separator.

Which half a token belongs to is marked by [[segment-embeddings]]. The question carries the A embedding and the passage carries B. That marker is added into each token's input vector along with its position, so the split is told to the encoder as a signal on every token, not only as a boundary symbol.

The text is not split into words. [[wordpiece-tokenization]] breaks rare words into pieces, so the positions the head will index are subword pieces. A gold answer string therefore has to be aligned onto piece boundaries before it can become a start index and an end index. Section 4.2 does not describe that alignment step.

The encoder then runs once over the whole packed thing. Because of [[bidirectional-self-attention]], a passage token's [[final-hidden-vector-ti]] is already a function of the question as well as of its own neighbourhood. The head that follows never reads the question directly. It only ever sees these vectors.

One constraint travels with the format. The packed sequence is bounded by the same [[max-sequence-length-512]] cap used during pre-training, so question and paragraph together have to fit inside it. The section says nothing about paragraphs that do not.

[[fig-4]] draws exactly this as one of its four panels: the same encoder, the question in the A slot, the passage in the B slot, and arrows leaving the passage positions.

chapters.title: Two softmaxes and where their gradients go
chapters.body:
The forward pass of [[span-prediction-head]] is two dot products per position, and nothing else.

Take [[start-and-end-vectors]]. For every paragraph position $i$, compute the scalar $S \cdot T_i$. That is one number per token, saying how good a start that token is. [[eq-span-start-probability]] then normalises those numbers into a distribution, $P_i = e^{S \cdot T_i} / \sum_j e^{S \cdot T_j}$.

The denominator is worth reading closely. The sum runs over the words of the paragraph, so the question's own positions are not candidate answers at all. The paper states that range in words and does not spell out the masking that enforces it.

$E$ does the same arithmetic to give an end distribution over the same set of positions.

The loss for one example is two cross-entropies added: $-\log P^{start}_{i^*} - \log P^{end}_{j^*}$, where $i^*$ and $j^*$ are the annotated start and end.

Now follow the gradients. The start term is the only thing that ever touches $S$. The end term is the only thing that ever touches $E$. Both terms flow down into every pre-trained weight, because fine-tuning trains the encoder end to end rather than only the new layer.

So the only place where a start and its end can be coordinated is inside $T$ itself. The head has no capacity to represent a relation between the two. If the predicted endpoints agree, it is because the encoder made those two vectors agree.

This is [[task-specific-output-layer]] in its thinnest form, and it is why the paper can claim [[minimal-task-specific-parameters]] for a token-level task as well as for a classification one. Compare [[mlm-output-softmax]], which projects each vector onto 30,000 classes; here there are two vectors and no matrix.

Fine-tuning on v1.1 runs 3 epochs at learning rate 5e-5 with batch size 32, inside the [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] grid used across the paper.

chapters.title: Searching pairs with an additive score
chapters.body:
At prediction time the head computes the same two scalars per position, then [[span-score-and-decoding]] searches. [[eq-span-score]] gives a candidate running from $i$ to $j$ the value $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$.

Three things follow from that form being a sum.

First, drop the constraint $j \geq i$ and the maximisation separates completely. The best pair would be the best start and the best end, each found on its own. The ordering constraint is the only thing coupling the two choices, and it couples them by forbidding pairs rather than by rescoring them.

Second, the raw sum ranks candidates the same way the two probabilities do. $\log P^{start}_i + \log P^{end}_j$ equals $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$ minus the two log-normalisers, and those two subtractions are the same number for every candidate within one example. The unnormalised score is therefore the log of the product of two independent distributions, up to a constant.

Third, a span's score does not depend on its width. Extending a candidate from three tokens to sixty changes the score only through whichever endpoint moved. There is no length term in the expression, and the description in section 4.2 sets no maximum. Under [[exact-match-and-f1]] an over-long prediction scores zero on Exact Match while [[f1-score]] still gives partial credit for the overlap.

What the head does not carry is the point of the comparison. [[prior-squad-systems]] built explicit attention machinery between question and passage into the model itself. Here all of that work has to have happened in the encoder before the head sees a single vector.

[[table-2]] is the evidence offered: 91.8 test F1 for a single model, 93.2 for the ensemble. Two caveats sit with it. [[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules]] let those entries train on any public data, so the paper first applies [[triviaqa-augmentation]] to match — worth only 0.1 to 0.4 F1 by its own account.

chapters.title: Letting the model decline
chapters.body:
[[squad-v2-0]] removes the guarantee that the paragraph contains the answer, which the paper calls a more realistic problem.

Take the construction first. [[cls-as-null-span]] declares that [[unanswerable-questions]] have a span starting and ending at the classification token, and both probability spaces are widened by that one position. Nothing else changes shape. The start softmax now runs over the paragraph plus that position, and an unanswerable training example is simply one whose annotated start and end are both it. The two cross-entropies stay the two cross-entropies.

Prediction adds one comparison. [[null-span-score]] is $s_{null} = S \cdot C + E \cdot C$, using [[final-hidden-vector-c]] where a passage vector would otherwise sit, so abstention is scored by the same two vectors as everything else.

Here is the part worth pausing on. If the null span were only another candidate in the search, the decision would be a plain argmax and no threshold would be needed at all. [[eq-null-answer-threshold]] instead demands that the best real span beat $s_{null}$ by a margin of [[tau-threshold]].

The margin exists because the training objective and the scoring metric are not the same thing. Likelihood treats a missed abstention and a wrong span alike. F1 does not. So one scalar is fitted afterwards, on [[dev-set-model-selection]], to place the operating point where F1 is highest. That metric has no gradient, so the scalar cannot be trained; the paper does not say how the search over it is run.

The reported result is [[table-3]]: 83.1 test F1 for a single BERT_LARGE against 78.0 for the best prior entry the authors count, an [[absolute-improvement]] of 5.1 points. Human performance in the same table is 89.5, so the remaining gap is wide. No TriviaQA data was used for this model, and fine-tuning ran 2 epochs at 5e-5 with batch size 48.

n-eleven-tasks-and-the-numbers--squad-la.title: Two vectors against a leaderboard
n-eleven-tasks-and-the-numbers--squad-la.intro: The parent gave you the shape of Table 2 and the two margins it is used to claim. This level counts the actual parameters the head adds, walks the recipe and what it cost, and then reads the table's cells against each other — including the places where the two metrics disagree and where a quoted margin does not fall out of any subtraction on the page.

chapters.title: Two thousand new numbers
chapters.body:
The passage reaches the encoder inside a [[packed-question-passage-sequence]], and what comes back is one top-layer vector per position, written $T_i$ — see [[final-hidden-vector-ti]].

The [[span-prediction-head]] adds two things to that and nothing else. [[start-and-end-vectors]] $S$ and $E$ each live in $\mathbb{R}^H$, where $H$ is the [[hidden-size-h]].

It is worth counting them. For BERT_LARGE, $H = 1024$, so $S$ and $E$ together are 2,048 numbers. The encoder beneath them holds 340 million — see [[bert-base-and-bert-large]]. The task-specific part is about six parameters in every million.

Now the forward pass. [[eq-span-start-probability]] sets the probability that token $i$ starts the answer to $P_i = e^{S \cdot T_i} / \sum_j e^{S \cdot T_j}$.

Read the denominator. The sum runs over the words of the paragraph, not over the whole sequence. The question's tokens are encoded, and every passage token attends to them, but a question token is never a candidate start. The end distribution uses the same formula with $E$ in place of $S$.

Training maximises the log-likelihood of the correct start plus the log-likelihood of the correct end. Those are two independent cross-entropies over the same passage.

Decoding is where they meet. [[eq-span-score]] scores a candidate as $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, an additive score, so the best start and the best end could be picked separately.

They are not. Picking separately can return $j < i$: an [[answer-span]] that ends before it begins. Hence the $j \geq i$ requirement in [[span-score-and-decoding]].

That constraint lives only at prediction time. Nothing in the training objective pushes against an inverted pair. The paper also states no maximum span length, so the search is over every ordered pair in the paragraph. This is what [[task-specific-output-layer]] amounts to here.

chapters.title: Three epochs, and where they sit in the grid
chapters.body:
Batch size 32, learning rate 5e-5, three epochs. Those numbers mean more once you see the menu they were chosen from.

The [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] grid offers batch size 16 or 32, Adam learning rate 5e-5, 3e-5 or 2e-5, and 2, 3 or 4 epochs. Dropout stays at 0.1 and everything else carries over from pre-training unchanged.

So SQuAD takes the largest batch and the largest learning rate on the menu, with the middle epoch count. That is a corner of the grid, not a midpoint.

The paper's own caveat softens what that choice means. It reports that datasets with 100k or more labeled examples were far less sensitive to hyperparameters than small ones — [[dataset-size-hyperparameter-sensitivity]]. [[squad-v1-1]] has roughly 100k question/answer pairs, so it sits at the edge of the band where the grid barely matters. The [[exhaustive-hyperparameter-search]] and the [[dev-set-model-selection]] behind it are cheap insurance here rather than the source of the score.

Now the cost. Three passes over 100k examples at batch 32 is about 3,125 steps per epoch, so roughly 9,400 updates in total.

Compare that to [[training-steps-and-epochs]]: one million updates during pre-training. Fine-tuning is under one percent of the steps, and it is [[end-to-end-fine-tuning]] — all 340 million parameters move during those 9,400.

A footnote attached to the [[fine-tuning-cost]] claim puts a wall-clock number on it: around 30 minutes on a single [[cloud-tpu]], which here is four chips, reaching 91.0 Dev F1.

That 91.0 is a tenth above the 90.9 the table reports for single BERT_LARGE. The paper does not reconcile the two figures.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Where EM and F1 name different winners
chapters.body:
Every row of [[table-2]] that reports both metrics shows the same ordering, F1 above EM. The size of that gap is the part worth reading.

[[exact-match-and-f1]] are computed against the reference answer string. EM is binary: the predicted string matches a reference or it does not. F1 is the [[f1-score]] over token overlap, so a prediction that catches the right words and one extra still scores well.

Walk the gaps down the table. BERT_BASE: $88.5 - 80.8 = 7.7$. Single BERT_LARGE: $90.9 - 84.1 = 6.8$. The submitted ensemble on Test: $93.2 - 87.4 = 5.8$.

The gap narrows as the scores rise. A system that is finding the right region more often is also cutting its boundaries more often in exactly the annotated place.

The human row has the widest gap of any row: $91.2 - 82.3 = 8.9$. People agree about which words answer the question far more often than they agree about where to trim it.

Then a case where the two metrics disagree outright. Among the [[prior-squad-systems]], R.M. Reader's ensemble reports 81.2 EM and 87.9 F1 on Dev. BERT_BASE reports 80.8 and 88.5.

So BERT_BASE is 0.6 F1 ahead and 0.4 EM behind, on the same pair of rows.

Every claim the paper makes about [[question-answering]] on this table is stated in F1. That is a defensible choice for extractive QA, and it is also the metric under which the smaller model wins that particular comparison. The [[absolute-improvement]] figures quoted in the text are all F1 differences.

chapters.title: Climbing the Dev column, then crossing to Test
chapters.body:
Five rows carry the BERT results, and only two of them reach the Test columns. The three Dev-only rows are the ladder; the two submitted rows are what the leaderboard sees.

First rung. BERT_BASE reaches 88.5 Dev F1 and BERT_LARGE reaches 90.9, a gain of 2.4 for going from 110 million parameters to 340 million. That 88.5 is the same figure that appears as BERT_BASE's SQuAD column in [[table-5]], and the pattern matches [[effect-of-model-size]].

Second rung. [[ensembling]] seven systems takes Dev F1 from 90.9 to 91.8, a gain of 0.9. The caption says the seven differ in pre-training checkpoint and in fine-tuning seed. Seed is doing real work there: the paper elsewhere reports [[fine-tuning-random-restarts]] because fine-tuning BERT_LARGE was sometimes unstable, and the same variability is being recruited here as diversity. Note that this is seven models for one task, not the usual [[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task]] multiplication.

Third rung. [[triviaqa-augmentation]] moves single Dev F1 from 90.9 to 91.1 and ensemble Dev F1 from 91.8 to 92.2. On EM the same two moves are 84.1 to 84.2 and 85.8 to 86.2.

Those four deltas are 0.2, 0.4, 0.1 and 0.4. That is exactly the "0.1-0.4 F1" the paper quotes as what it would lose by dropping TriviaQA.

Now the crossing. The single submitted system goes 91.1 Dev to 91.8 Test, up 0.7. The ensemble goes 92.2 to 93.2, up 1.0.

Test comes in above Dev both times. R.M. Reader does the same, 87.9 Dev to 88.5 Test. So the lift is a property of the split, not of BERT — and reading the Dev-only rows as if they were Test numbers understates them by about a point.

chapters.title: The 1.5, the 1.3, and the fine print
chapters.body:
The comparison block is dated: Top Leaderboard Systems, December 10th 2018. nlnet's ensemble sits at 86.0 Test EM and 91.7 Test F1. QANet's ensemble sits at 84.5 and 90.5. The human row sits at 82.3 and 91.2.

The ensemble margin is a clean subtraction. $93.2 - 91.7 = 1.5$.

The single-system margin is not. Against nlnet, $91.8 - 91.7 = 0.1$. The only difference of 1.3 anywhere in the table is $91.8 - 90.5$, against QANet, the #2 entry. The paper does not say that is the comparison it means, and from the table alone the +1.3 cannot be reconstructed.

What the table does support is the sharper sentence: one BERT at 91.8 Test F1 edges past the best ensemble on the board at 91.7. The qualification "in terms of F1 score" matters. On Test EM the same single system reads 85.1 against nlnet's 86.0, and is 0.9 behind.

Two pieces of fine print sit under all of this. [[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules]] means the top entries have no current public description and may train on any public data. A footnote adds that QANet is described in a published paper but has improved substantially since. So the strongest comparison points are systems whose current form is undocumented, and TriviaQA is the paper's way of matching the data allowance rather than disputing it.

The Published block is different in kind. BiDAF+ELMo reaches 85.8 Test F1 — a reading-comprehension [[task-specific-architecture]] with [[elmo]] features fed in, an instance of the [[feature-based-approach]]. R.M. Reader's ensemble reaches 88.5.

Both carry hand-built [[bidirectional-cross-attention]] between question and passage. BERT's argument, [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention]], is that the concatenated encoding already does that, leaving [[minimal-task-specific-parameters]] on top. Against the best published row, 91.8 is 3.3 ahead.

n-what-each-piece-is-worth--two-ladders.title: Two ladders: more layers, more steps
n-what-each-piece-is-worth--two-ladders.intro: The parent read both ladders top to bottom. This level reads the first one as a set of differences instead — which steps hold everything else fixed, which one does not, and what the perplexity column is actually measuring. It then opens up the fine-tuning protocol behind the accuracies, the arithmetic under the small-data hypothesis, and the per-step signal deficit that the second ladder was drawn to test.

chapters.title: Six runs, and which comparisons are clean
chapters.body:
Every row of [[table-6|the table]] is a separate pre-training run from scratch. Not six checkpoints from one run: six times through the whole [[pre-training-procedure|pre-training procedure]], same corpus, same optimizer, same schedule, differing only in the three numbers at the left.

Those three are [[model-size-notation|L, H and A]]. Note that [[hidden-size-h|H]] does more than set the width of what passes between layers, because each block's feed-forward network is [[feed-forward-filter-size|four times H wide]] inside. Raising H therefore raises per-layer cost quadratically, while raising L raises it linearly.

The LM (ppl) column is not a downstream score. It is held-out perplexity on the masked-prediction objective itself — the exponentiated mean cross-entropy of [[mlm-output-softmax|the output softmax over the vocabulary]], on positions the model was asked to fill. So one column reports how well pre-training went, and three report what transferred.

Now read the rows as differences. Rows one and three hold H=768 and A=12 and double L from 3 to 6: [[mnli|MNLI]] goes 77.9 to 81.9, a gain of 4.0. Rows three and four double again, 6 to 12: 81.9 to 84.4, a gain of 2.5. Rows five and six double once more, 12 to 24 at H=1024: 85.7 to 86.6, a gain of 0.9.

Three doublings of depth, each buying less than the one before it.

One step is not clean. Moving from row four to row five raises H from 768 to 1024 and A from 12 to 16 at the same time. Width is never varied on its own anywhere in the table.

The paper reports parameter counts only for [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE]], 110M and 340M. The four other rows are given as configurations, not as sizes. And the prose claims strict improvement "across all four datasets", where the table prints three accuracy columns — [[mrpc|MRPC]] and [[sst-2|SST-2]] alongside MNLI — plus the perplexity.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: The row where only the split changes
chapters.body:
The A=3 and A=12 rows at L=6, H=768 are the one place the table isolates head count. Worth being precise about what a head is here, because the change costs nothing.

Inside a block of the [[transformer-encoder|Transformer encoder]], [[self-attention|self-attention]] projects each position into A query, key and value vectors of size H/A, runs A separate attentions, concatenates the results back to width H, and projects once more. With H fixed at 768, going from 3 heads to 12 repartitions the same 768 dimensions: three subspaces of 256, or twelve of 64. The projection matrices have the same total shape either way.

So the two runs hold parameter count fixed. What changes is how many separate attention distributions each layer computes — three softmaxes over the sequence per layer, or twelve. Each of them is [[bidirectional-self-attention|unmasked in both directions]], which is what makes [[deep-bidirectionality|bidirectionality at every layer]] a property of every head rather than of the stack's top.

The move buys a perplexity drop of 5.24 to 4.68, close to eleven percent relative. On MNLI it buys 1.3 points, which is about half of what doubling depth from 6 to 12 buys at the next step down the table.

The paper does not discuss this row. [[ablation-studies|The ablation section]] frames itself around size, and head count at fixed H is not a size change in that sense.

It is also one run against one run. The two configurations differ by a whole pre-training run, so nothing printed separates the head count from run-to-run variation in pre-training itself. Both of the paper's headline configurations keep the per-head dimension at 64, which makes the A=3 row the odd one out rather than the norm it departs from.

chapters.title: What averaging five restarts hides
chapters.body:
A restart here is narrower than it sounds. The pre-trained checkpoint is held fixed; what varies is the shuffling of the fine-tuning data and the initialization of the classifier layer.

That layer is the whole task model. For a GLUE classification task it is [[c-vector-classification-head|one matrix W of shape K by H]] applied to the final [CLS] vector, and it is the only weight set that starts from noise — the design goal of [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|adding as few new weights as possible]], with everything else carried over and trained on by [[end-to-end-fine-tuning|end-to-end fine-tuning]].

Walk the size of it on MRPC. Two labels, H=1024, so 2,048 fresh weights against 340M pre-trained ones. [[glue-fine-tuning-protocol|The protocol]] uses batch 32 for 3 epochs, so 3,600 examples give about 113 updates per epoch and roughly 340 in total.

The entire spread between restarts comes from those two thousand weights and the order of those few hundred minibatches. It was large enough to matter: the headline runs used [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|several restarts and kept the best on Dev]], selected on [[dev-set-model-selection|the development split]].

Table 6 averages five instead of keeping the best of five. Two consequences follow.

First, its cells are not comparable to [[table-1|the GLUE scoreboard]], which reports Test scores under best-of-restart selection. Second, the ladder's gains cannot have been inflated by restart selection, because no selection happened.

What is missing is any measure of spread. Means are printed, standard deviations and ranges are not. The top step of the ladder is 0.9 on MNLI and 0.9 on MRPC, and whether that clears restart noise cannot be checked from the table. The steps lower down are several points, so it matters less there. [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|The learning rate was also chosen per task on Dev]], and whether that search was rerun for each row is not stated.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: The claim resting on 3,600 examples
chapters.body:
On the largest task in the table the scaling result was never in dispute. Bigger models had long been known to help machine translation and language modeling, and the perplexity column shows the same thing happening here.

The contested case is MRPC: 79.8 at the bottom of the ladder, 87.8 at the top, eight points on 3,600 labeled examples of a task the paper calls substantially different from what pre-training does. That is one of the [[low-resource-tasks|small-data tasks]] where training a deep model from scratch is not an option.

[[prior-scaling-evidence|The earlier evidence]] pointed the other way, and it is worth seeing why the paper thinks it can be set aside. Peters et al. raised a bi-LM from two layers to four and got mixed downstream results. Melamud et al. found [[hidden-size-h|hidden size]] 600 beat 200, and 1,000 beat neither.

Both used the [[feature-based-approach|feature-based approach]]. The pre-trained model is frozen, its vectors are fed into a [[task-specific-architecture|hand-built task architecture]], and that architecture is trained from scratch — the arrangement [[elmo|ELMo]] uses.

[[few-random-parameters-hypothesis|The paper's explanation]] turns on that difference. A fresh task network has to learn how to use richer features from the labeled data alone, and 3,600 examples is not much to learn a usage policy with. Under [[fine-tuning-approach|the fine-tuning approach]] almost nothing is fresh, so the labeled data only has to move a solution the encoder already holds.

The paper writes this as a hypothesis, and the hedge is fair. No run varies the count of randomly initialized parameters while holding model size fixed. Section 5.3 does freeze BERT and train a fresh network on top — [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|the feature-based version of BERT]] — but at one size only, so it does not give the second ladder the hypothesis would need. And the prior systems differ in objective, corpus and architecture as well as in transfer strategy.

chapters.title: The second ladder, and what its two curves share
chapters.body:
[[effect-of-number-of-training-steps|The steps ablation]] asks a different question with the same instrument: hold the model at BERT_BASE, and fine-tune from checkpoints saved at k pre-training steps. [[fig-5|The figure]] plots MNLI Dev accuracy against k.

The curve's shape matters more than its endpoint. The first plotted checkpoint sits near 78.7, 200k reaches about 82.2, 400k about 83.2, 600k about 84.0, and 1M about 84.4.

The first 200k steps buy roughly three and a half points. The last 400k buy roughly four tenths of one.

So the paper's answer — almost 1.0 more accuracy at 1M than at 500k — is a claim about the flat part of the curve. That part is not cheap. [[training-steps-and-epochs|The full run]] is a million updates at 128,000 tokens per batch, about forty passes over 3.3 billion words, four days on the paper's [[cloud-tpu|TPU]] configuration. Half of that time buys under a point on this task.

The second question is about convergence. [[masked-language-model|The masked objective]] scores a prediction at only [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% of positions]] per sequence. At 256 sequences of 512 tokens that is roughly 19,200 targets per step, against about 128,000 for a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right model]] that predicts at every position — about one target in seven. [[mlm-convergence-cost|The worry]] is that this makes each step worth less.

The curves say it does, slightly. The masked line starts below the left-to-right line at the first checkpoint, near 78.7 against 79.4. It crosses before 100k and finishes about 2.2 points above, 84.4 against 82.2.

One caution about the comparison. The left-to-right curve is [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|the LTR & No NSP model]], which drops [[next-sentence-prediction]] as well as masking, so the gap between the curves is not the masking objective alone. A second: C.1 quotes 128,000 words per batch throughout, while [[sequence-length-schedule|the length schedule]] runs 90% of steps at length 128, and the appendix does not say whether the batch was widened in sequences to compensate.

n-what-each-piece-is-worth--frozen-encod.title: Freezing the encoder, and what that setting exposes
n-what-each-piece-is-worth--frozen-encod.intro: The parent gave the outcome: 0.3 F1, and a masking mixture defended by 0.9 F1. This level gives the machinery underneath. Why a frozen BERT is worth wanting at all, what the tagging setup does and does not include, what the frozen side has to add back before it can compete, and what the two tables look like read one row at a time.

chapters.title: Two reasons to want a frozen BERT
chapters.body:
The paper does not run this experiment only to price fine-tuning. Section 5.3 opens by naming two advantages that [[feature-based-approach|keeping the pre-trained model fixed and feeding its outputs into a separate model]] holds over [[fine-tuning-approach|training every pre-trained parameter on the task]].

The first is architectural. Not every task can be expressed as text in, vectors out of a [[transformer-encoder|Transformer encoder]]. Some need a model built for their particular shape, and that [[task-specific-architecture|hand-designed component]] has to sit somewhere. If BERT is usable only by fine-tuning, those tasks cannot use BERT at all.

The second is computational. A frozen encoder's outputs depend on nothing but the input text. So you can run BERT over the training set once, store [[contextual-representations|the vectors it produces]], and then train many cheap models on top of that stored file. Fine-tuning offers no such reuse. Every experiment pays the encoder's forward and backward pass again.

Both advantages already belong to [[elmo|ELMo]], the feature-based model BERT is set against throughout the paper.

So this is not simply one more entry in [[ablation-studies|the ablation programme]]. [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|The frozen run]] asks whether BERT can be used in the mode its main rival is used in.

That framing also fixes what counts as success. The frozen setup does not have to win. It has to land close enough that the mode is worth using.

chapters.title: The task, configured
chapters.body:
[[conll-2003-ner|The benchmark]] is a [[named-entity-recognition|token-labelling]] shared task. Every token carries a tag saying whether it falls inside a person, organisation, location or miscellaneous name, and whether it begins one. It is a [[token-level-tasks|per-token task]], so the output layer reads one vector per position rather than a single pooled vector.

Three configuration choices are worth stating, because each is a decision rather than a default.

Case preserving. The paper specifies a case-preserving [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]] model. Naming that implies the alternative it is departing from, where the text is lowercased before tokenisation. Capitalisation is one of the strongest surface cues for a name in English, and lowercasing discards it.

Maximal document context. CoNLL sentences are drawn from news documents. The paper feeds as much surrounding document as the data supplies, rather than one sentence at a time. That fits because [[max-sequence-length-512|a sequence may run to 512 tokens]].

No CRF. Tagging systems normally put a conditional random field over the output. A CRF scores whole tag sequences, so it can rule out illegal transitions — an inside-person tag directly after a begin-organisation tag, say. Removing it means each token's tag is picked independently by [[task-specific-output-layer|one linear layer]]. [[tagging-without-crf|The paper drops it]] on purpose, so that the score reflects the representation rather than a decoder doing repair work afterwards.

One alignment detail closes the setup. WordPiece splits rare words into several pieces, but the labels are per word. The classifier reads [[first-sub-token-classification|the final vector of the first piece only]], and [[final-hidden-vector-ti|the remaining pieces' vectors]] receive no loss at all.

chapters.title: What the frozen side has to add back
chapters.body:
The extraction is literal. Activations are read out of one or more layers with no gradient reaching BERT, so [[end-to-end-fine-tuning|the joint training of encoder and head]] is switched off entirely.

That leaves a problem the fine-tuned side does not have. A fine-tuned BERT can reshape its own upper layers to suit NER. A frozen one cannot. Whatever adaptation the task needs has to happen above the extracted vectors.

So the paper inserts [[frozen-feature-bilstm-classifier|a two-layer BiLSTM of hidden size 768]] between the features and the classifier, [[bilstm|reading the sequence in both directions]] and initialised at random. That BiLSTM and the classifier are the only trained parameters.

Count what each side learns from scratch. The fine-tuned run adds a single linear layer, which is [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|about as few new weights as the design allows]]. The frozen run adds two [[lstm|recurrent]] layers at [[hidden-size-h|the same width the encoder itself uses]], trained on CoNLL's labels alone.

So the table is not comparing frozen BERT against fine-tuned BERT with everything else held constant. It compares frozen BERT plus a fresh recurrent model against fine-tuned BERT plus a linear layer.

The frozen side is carrying extra trainable machinery. That makes the small gap easier to reach, and harder to charge cleanly to the representation.

The paper has used this move before. [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|A randomly initialised BiLSTM]] was stacked on [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|the left-to-right ablation]] in Section 5.1, there to supply the right-side context that encoder could not see. Both times the BiLSTM patches something the encoder is not permitted to do for itself.

chapters.title: Six ways to read twelve layers
chapters.body:
[[layer-selection-ablation|Which activations to tap]] becomes a free choice once the encoder is frozen, and [[table-7|the NER table]] spends six rows on it. All six use BERT_BASE, so twelve layers are on offer, and all six report Dev [[f1-score|F1]].

Start at the floor. Feeding the embeddings alone — [[input-embedding-sum|the token, segment and position vectors summed]], before any [[self-attention|attention]] has run — gives 91.0. That is the score with no contextualisation whatsoever, 5.1 points below the best row.

Then the two single-layer rows. The last hidden layer gives 94.9, the second-to-last gives 95.6. The top layer is 0.7 worse than the one directly beneath it, and the paper offers no account of why.

Then the combinations. A weighted sum of the last four layers gives 95.9. Concatenating those same four gives 96.1. The two differ in width: the sum collapses four 768-dimensional vectors into one, while [[concat-last-four-layers|the concatenation]] hands the BiLSTM a 3072-dimensional input and leaves the weighing to it.

More layers is not simply better. A weighted sum over all twelve gives 95.5, below the four-layer sum and below the second-to-last layer taken alone.

Two numbers for scale. ELMo's Dev F1 here is 95.7, so two of the six frozen settings beat it and four do not. [[bert-base-and-bert-large|Fine-tuned BERT_BASE]] sits at 96.4.

The evidence is thinner than six rows make it look. Every number is on Dev, hyperparameters were selected on [[dev-set-model-selection|that same split]], and adjacent rows differ by 0.2. The caption does say each score is averaged over five random restarts, which is a stronger report than [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|the GLUE protocol of keeping the best restart]].

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: The masking mixture, row by row
chapters.body:
[[masking-procedure-ablation|The second ablation]] borrows the frozen setting rather than studying it. Its subject is [[masked-language-model|the masked LM objective]], specifically what happens to a token after [[masking-rate-15-percent|the 15% draw]] has selected it for prediction.

Three things can happen, and [[mask-same-rnd-strategies|the paper names them]]. MASK substitutes [[mask-token|the placeholder]]. SAME leaves the token untouched. RND swaps in a random vocabulary item. In all three cases the original token is the prediction target. Six pre-training runs vary the three probabilities and change nothing else.

Read [[table-8|the table]] as three result columns.

Fine-tuned MNLI spans 83.6 to 84.4 across all six runs. The best is 80% MASK with 20% SAME and no RND, at 84.4. A run using MASK every time scores 84.3. [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|The shipped mixture]] scores 84.2, third on [[mnli|this task]] behind both.

Fine-tuned NER spans 94.8 to 95.4, and here the shipped mixture is highest.

Frozen NER is the column the section exists for. The shipped mixture gives 94.9 and MASK-only gives 94.0. The other four rows cluster between 94.6 and 94.7, so the effect is one row rather than a trend across the mixtures.

[[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|The explanation offered]] rests on [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|the gap between pre-training conditions and downstream conditions]]. A fine-tuned model can adjust its representations to inputs containing no placeholder. A frozen one never gets the chance.

Two cautions. The paper also calls RND-only much worse, but that row reads 94.6 frozen, 0.3 off the shipped mixture. And this table's best fine-tuned NER score is 95.4 where Table 7's is 96.4, so the two tables are not on the same footing, and the paper does not say why.

n-the-data-problem--word-types-to-occurr.title: The same trick on bigger units
n-the-data-problem--word-types-to-occurr.intro: The parent named the three sentence-level objectives. This level takes each apart into what you would have to build to run it, what its training signal can and cannot press the fixed vector to encode, and what it costs per step — then follows the two that come back in BERT's own design far enough to see exactly what was kept and what was dropped.

chapters.title: Ranking, and who sets the difficulty
chapters.body:
Consider what a ranking objective needs before it can produce a single gradient.

First, true pairs. Those are free in running text, provided the corpus is stored as documents rather than as a shuffled bag of sentences. BERT's own recipe insists on exactly that later, calling a [[document-level-corpus]] necessary and naming the [[billion-word-benchmark]] as the kind of shuffled data it deliberately avoids. Any objective built on the phrase "the sentence that followed" carries the same requirement.

Second, negatives. These are sampled: other sentences pulled from elsewhere in the corpus. Nothing marks them as wrong answers. Their wrongness is an artifact of where the sampler drew them from.

Third, a score per candidate and a normalization across the candidate set. The true successor's score is pushed up relative to the sampled ones, which is where "ranks" comes from. Nothing in the objective asks for a calibrated probability that B follows A — only that B beat the alternatives on offer.

Now the part the paper does not discuss, and which is a reading rather than a report. The difficulty of that comparison is set entirely by the sampler. Draw negatives uniformly from a large corpus and most of them are about something else entirely. A representation that encodes roughly what the sentence is about already wins, and gradient descent has no reason to push it further. Sharpen the sampler — negatives from the same document, or the same paragraph — and the identical objective demands much more.

Cheapness is the compensation. No decoder is trained and no distribution over the vocabulary is ever computed; the cost is one encoding pass per candidate plus a softmax over a handful of scores. For a [[downstream-task]] that will only ever see the resulting [[sentence-embeddings]], that is a small price for a signal drawn entirely from [[unlabeled-text]].

How easily this discrimination is actually won is something the paper does put a number on, for its own version. That comes two chapters down.

chapters.title: Generation, and the uneven pressure on the vector
chapters.body:
The generating objective replaces comparison with reconstruction.

Sentence A is encoded to one fixed-size vector. That vector is handed to a decoder, which emits the words of sentence B one at a time, left to right, each word conditioned on the vector and on the words already emitted. The loss is the cross entropy of the true next sentence under that decoder, summed over its words.

Every one of those per-word terms sends gradient back through the decoder and into the single vector. The vector is the only channel between the two sentences. Nothing about A can reach any prediction about B except through it.

That is a stronger demand than ranking makes, and a differently shaped one. Ranking asks the vector to sit far from the wrong candidates. Generation asks it to be informative enough to license specific words.

But the pressure is uneven, and this again is reading rather than paper. A left-to-right decoder gets a great deal right from its own prefix alone: agreement, function words, the completion of a phrase it has already started. Those predictions barely consult the vector, so they barely push on it. What the vector is really being asked to carry is the content the prefix cannot supply.

Cost runs the opposite way from ranking. There is a second network to train, and a distribution over the whole vocabulary to compute at every generated position — the expensive part of any [[left-to-right-language-model]]. BERT's own vocabulary softmax is 30,000-wide ([[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k]], [[mlm-output-softmax]]), and it pays that cost at masked positions only. A generating objective pays it at every position of the target sentence. The encoders and decoders of this period were typically [[lstm]] stacks.

Note where the one-directional shape sits here. It is in the decoder, on the output side. The paper's later objection, the [[unidirectionality-constraint]], concerns something else: what the pre-trained representation itself is allowed to condition on.

chapters.title: Denoising, and the line BERT draws against it
chapters.body:
The third family corrupts and restores.

A sentence goes in damaged. The target is the original sentence, undamaged. The paper names this family in a single clause and never says what the corruption is, so treat the particular noise as unspecified.

What the objective forces is easy to state. Whatever the encoder compresses the corrupted sentence into has to be enough to rebuild all of it: every word, in order, including the parts no later task will care about. Reconstruction does not get to choose what matters.

That is exactly what BERT's first objective is defined against. Section 3.1 draws the [[denoising-autoencoder-contrast]] in one sentence — the [[masked-language-model]] predicts only the masked words rather than reconstructing the entire input.

Walk what that changes. Under the [[masking-rate-15-percent]], a 128-token sequence has about 19 positions selected for prediction. The loss therefore has 19 terms. The other 109 tokens are input only: read, attended over, never scored. Full reconstruction of the same sequence would carry 128 terms, close to seven times as many.

Two things follow.

One: there is no bottleneck anywhere. Nothing is squeezed through a fixed-size vector, because the model is never asked to emit the sequence. Each position keeps its own vector, [[final-hidden-vector-ti]], and what gets read at a masked slot is that slot's vector alone.

Two: fewer scored positions means fewer gradient terms per step. The paper accepts that as a price — [[mlm-convergence-cost]] is its own admission that the masked objective converges more slowly than a left-to-right one.

The older name for filling a deleted word back in is the [[cloze-task]], which the paper notes is what its masked LM amounts to. The [[mask-token]] is what marks the deletion.

chapters.title: The ranking objective, rebuilt as a label
chapters.body:
Now the return. BERT's [[next-sentence-prediction]] is the ranking family's descendant, and the paper says so directly: NSP is closely related to the representation-learning objectives of Jernite et al. and Logeswaran and Lee.

Here is the instantiated version. Two spans are packed into one sequence as A and B — and "sentence" here means [[sentence-as-arbitrary-span]], any stretch of contiguous text rather than a linguistic unit. Half the time B is the span that actually followed A. Half the time B is a span sampled from elsewhere in the corpus. The two cases are labeled [[isnext-notnext]]. The decision is read off [[final-hidden-vector-c]], the top-layer vector at the first position.

The shape has changed. A ranking objective compares candidates against each other; NSP judges one pair in isolation and returns a bit. The negatives are sampled the same way. The decision is not.

Footnote 5 gives the number the earlier chapters wanted: the final model reaches 97-98% accuracy on NSP. Whatever discrimination corpus-sampled negatives require, the trained model makes it nearly every time.

That the task is easy does not settle whether it helps, and the paper tests that separately. [[table-5]] pre-trains a model identically except for dropping NSP. [[qnli]] falls from 88.4 to 84.9, a drop of 3.5 points. The other columns move much less: MNLI 84.4 to 83.9, SQuAD 88.5 to 87.9, SST-2 92.7 to 92.6 — half a point, six tenths, one tenth.

The paper's summary is that removing NSP hurts performance significantly on QNLI, MNLI and SQuAD 1.1. The QNLI number is what carries that sentence. The other two are inside a point, and worth reading as such.

The stated motivation is that [[question-answering]] and [[natural-language-inference]] turn on the relationship between two texts, which single-sentence language modeling never has to represent.

chapters.title: The objectives borrowed, the deliverable dropped
chapters.body:
The objectives survived. What changed is what leaves pre-training.

The paper puts the difference in one sentence: in prior work only [[sentence-embeddings]] are transferred downstream, where BERT transfers all parameters to initialize end-task model parameters. That is [[full-parameter-transfer-vs-sentence-embeddings]].

Unpack the two deliverables.

In the sentence-embedding setting the product is a vector per span. Train the objective once, run the encoder over your task's text, keep the vectors, build the task model on top. The encoder's weights never move again — that is the [[feature-based-approach]]. It also explains why so much design effort went into the objective itself. The vector is all you get, so it has to be good unaided.

BERT ships weights instead. All 110M parameters of BERT_BASE, or all 340M of BERT_LARGE, become the initialization of the task model, and [[end-to-end-fine-tuning]] moves every one of them on the labeled data. The only parameters starting from scratch are one matrix: [[c-vector-classification-head]], $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$ for a $K$-way task.

Which makes the footnote consistent rather than surprising. Footnote 6 says the pre-trained [[cls-token]] vector is not a meaningful sentence representation without fine-tuning, because it was trained with [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] — [[c-not-a-sentence-representation]].

Take that at face value. The artifact this whole line of work set out to produce, a fixed vector standing for a span and useful as it stands, is the one thing BERT declines to claim. Its first position was trained to answer a single binary question, and nothing in pre-training asked it to be more than that.

So the borrowing runs one way. BERT takes the objectives and leaves the deliverable, which is what places it in the [[fine-tuning-approach]] column rather than as another entry in the sentence-embedding line.

n-only-one-side--the-picture-and-its-con.title: Four times the text, at the same number of passes
n-only-one-side--the-picture-and-its-con.intro: The parent settled the arithmetic: 3.3 billion words, a million steps, roughly forty passes either way. This level goes underneath it — what the two corpora actually contain, why the paper insists the text arrive as documents, how one training sequence is assembled out of that text, and what the length schedule does to the run it describes.

chapters.title: What the 3.3 billion words are made of
chapters.body:
BERT's [[pre-training-data]] is two collections, not one, and they are unequal.

[[bookscorpus]] is 800M words of unpublished books, cited to Zhu et al. (2015). [[english-wikipedia-corpus]] is 2,500M words. Divide: $2{,}500 / 3{,}300 \approx 0.76$. About three-quarters of the text the model reads is encyclopedia prose.

The paper describes exactly one filtering step, and only for the Wikipedia half. It extracts "only the text passages" and ignores lists, tables and headers.

Think about what that removes. An infobox goes. A bulleted filmography goes. A section heading goes, which means the running text arrives without the scaffolding that told a human reader where a topic started.

What is left is paragraphs. It is [[unlabeled-text]] in the sense the [[language-model-pre-training]] literature uses the term: nobody annotated it, and the whole training signal comes from the text predicting parts of itself.

One thing the paper does not state is how the two corpora are mixed when sequences are sampled. Sampling in proportion to size would put Wikipedia in roughly three sequences out of four. Some other weighting is possible. The appendix says only "the corpus", as if it were one thing.

There is a second silence worth naming. The books half is shared with [[openai-gpt]], so everything BERT added is Wikipedia specifically.

That added text differs from BooksCorpus in two ways at once: there is more of it, and it is a different genre — expository articles rather than narrative fiction. The paper treats the difference as a quantity. It never separates the volume from the genre.

chapters.title: Why the text has to arrive as documents
chapters.body:
Section 3.1's data paragraph ends on the strongest word in it. Using a [[document-level-corpus]] rather than a shuffled sentence-level one is called "critical", and the named counter-example is the [[billion-word-benchmark]] — a corpus whose sentences have been shuffled, so that no sentence stands next to the one that originally followed it.

The stated reason is "in order to extract long contiguous sequences". Three parts of the recipe depend on that.

The first is [[next-sentence-prediction]]. Half of the pairs in every batch must be genuine successors, the [[isnext-notnext]] labels being balanced 50/50. In a shuffled corpus there is no successor to find. The positive class cannot be constructed at all, so the task is not made harder — it becomes unavailable.

The second is length. Spans are drawn up to a combined [[max-sequence-length-512]] tokens. A corpus of isolated sentences averaging a few dozen words has nothing that long to hand over, whatever its total size.

The third is what the sequence is worth once built. The [[masked-language-model]] objective lets a masked position attend only within its own sequence. Short sequences mean each prediction has less surrounding text to draw on.

Now the evidence. This is asserted, not measured.

BERT's [[ablation-studies]] remove pre-training objectives and vary model size. None of them swaps the corpus for a shuffled one and reports the drop. So "critical" here states the authors' design reasoning, and the reader has no number attached to it.

chapters.title: Assembling a single training example
chapters.body:
Appendix A.2 gives the generator as an ordered procedure. Following the order is the point, because each step constrains the next.

First, sample two spans of text from the corpus. The paper calls them "sentences" and warns in the same breath that they are "typically much longer than single sentences (but can be shorter also)" — the convention it labels [[sentence-as-arbitrary-span]].

Second, assign them. The first span takes the A [[segment-embeddings]] vector, the second takes B. That is [[sentence-pair-packing]]: one token sequence, opened by [[cls-token]], with [[sep-token]] marking the join and the end.

Third, flip the [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] coin. Half the time B is the span that actually followed A; half the time it is a random span from elsewhere.

Fourth, the length constraint. The two are sampled "such that the combined length is ≤512 tokens". Note where this sits: the cap acts during sampling, so the pair is drawn to fit rather than drawn and then cut short.

Fifth, tokenize and mask. Masking is applied after [[wordpiece-tokenization]], at a uniform [[masking-rate-15-percent]], with "no special consideration given to partial word pieces".

That last clause deserves unpacking. A rare word split into three pieces contributes three independently maskable positions.

So a mask can land on the middle piece while its two neighbours stay visible. Recovering it from the pieces on either side is a far easier prediction than recovering a whole word from its sentence. The paper names this and does not correct for it.

One sampled pair feeds both objectives at once, which is what [[combined-pretraining-loss]] adds up; [[masking-recipe-80-10-10]] decides what each chosen position is actually replaced by.

chapters.title: Nine hundred thousand short steps, then a hundred thousand long ones
chapters.body:
The [[sequence-length-schedule]] runs 90% of steps at length 128 and the last 10% at 512. The reason given for the short phase is speed, and the mechanism is [[attention-quadratic-cost]].

Walk that cost. [[self-attention]] scores every pair of positions in every layer. At length 128 that is $128^2 = 16{,}384$ scores per head per layer. At 512 it is $512^2 = 262{,}144$.

Sixteen times the attention work for four times the text. Per token, four times as expensive.

The reason given for the final phase is a different kind of reason. Those last 100,000 steps run at 512 "to learn the positional embeddings".

Here is why they have to. [[position-embeddings]] are one learned vector per slot in the sequence, folded into each token's input by [[input-embedding-sum]]. During a length-128 phase, slots 128 through 511 never occur in any input.

So their vectors receive no gradient whatsoever for 900,000 steps. They sit at initialization while everything else trains.

The consequence is worth stating flatly: the machinery that lets BERT read the far end of a long sequence gets a tenth of the run.

A.2 also states the ≤512 sampling cap and the schedule in separate paragraphs without reconciling them. During the short phase the effective cap must be 128, not 512, but the appendix never says so.

And the price, in hardware. [[training-steps-and-epochs]] costs four days per run. The two sizes in [[bert-base-and-bert-large]] got different machines for it: BASE on 4 Cloud TPUs, LARGE on 16. A [[cloud-tpu]] here is four chips, so 16 chips against 64 — roughly four times the hardware for roughly three times the parameters, at the same wall clock.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: Whether a million steps were needed
chapters.body:
Appendix C.1 asks the question in the reader's mouth: does BERT really need 128,000 words per batch times 1,000,000 steps?

The experiment behind [[effect-of-number-of-training-steps]] is simple. Take pre-training checkpoints at various step counts $k$, fine-tune each one on [[mnli]], and plot the resulting Dev accuracy. That plot is [[fig-5]].

The answer given is yes. BERT_BASE gains "almost 1.0% additional accuracy" going from 500k steps to 1M.

Read the shape as well as the number. A point of accuracy for doubling the run is a modest return, but the curve has not flattened — at a million steps it is still rising.

C.1's second question is about the objective rather than the budget. [[masked-language-model|Masked LM]] supplies a training target at only 15% of positions per sequence, where a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]] supplies one at every token, so MLM gets fewer gradient signals per step. That is [[mlm-convergence-cost]].

The paper concedes the point partly. MLM does converge slightly slower than the [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation]] model. But in absolute accuracy it says MLM overtakes LTR almost immediately, so the slower convergence never costs anything measurable at the end.

Two cautions on how far this carries.

It is one task, one model size, on a [[dev-set-model-selection]] split. Nothing here tests BERT_LARGE, or span extraction.

And the checkpoints are not what a shorter budget would produce. [[pretraining-optimizer-settings]] warm the learning rate over 10,000 steps and then decay it linearly. A checkpoint at 500k was caught mid-decay with its learning rate still well above where it ends, not trained to completion on a half-sized budget. Figure 5 is a curve through one run, not a comparison of runs. The full recipe sits on [[pre-training-procedure]].

n-turning-it-into-a-task-model--the-span.title: Letting the model decline
n-turning-it-into-a-task-model--the-span.intro: The level above gave the shape of the SQuAD 2.0 extension. This one walks the arithmetic underneath it: which index set each softmax actually runs over, what an unanswerable example's gradient pushes on, why the decision is a margin rather than a comparison, and what the reported 5.1 points do and do not rest on.

chapters.title: One more position in the same softmax
chapters.body:
The input to [[squad-v2-0]] is built exactly as before. Question in the A slot, passage in the B slot, one [[packed-question-passage-sequence]] through the encoder. Nothing about the input side is touched.

What changes is the index set the normalisation runs over.

In v1.1, [[eq-span-start-probability]] normalises $S \cdot T_i$ over the passage tokens only. The [[cls-token]] sits at position 0, and its final vector is not among the candidates. Under [[cls-as-null-span]] that position joins the pool. The denominator gains one term, $e^{S \cdot C}$, where $C$ is [[final-hidden-vector-c]]. The end softmax gains the matching term built from $E$.

Now take a training example from the [[unanswerable-questions]] set. Its annotated [[answer-span]] has start 0 and end 0. Run it forward, take the cross-entropy at the start index, take the cross-entropy at the end index, add the two. That is the same loss the answerable examples use. Nothing in the objective branches on which kind of question it is.

Follow where that gradient goes. It raises $S \cdot C$ and $E \cdot C$ while lowering $S \cdot T_i$ and $E \cdot T_j$ at every passage position. So [[start-and-end-vectors]] are trained by unanswerable examples as well, and so is the encoder beneath them, since $C$ and every [[final-hidden-vector-ti]] are functions of the whole sequence.

Count the parameters this extension adds. Zero. $S$ and $E$ were already the only task-specific weights, and [[minimal-task-specific-parameters]] holds unchanged.

One detail worth naming: on SQuAD there is no classification head, so $C$ had no consumer at all in v1.1. The null slot gives it one.

chapters.title: Why a margin and not an argmax
chapters.body:
With position 0 now inside both distributions, the search in [[span-score-and-decoding]] could simply include it. [[eq-span-score]] scores any pair as $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$. Set $i = j = 0$ and that expression is $S \cdot C + E \cdot C$, which is exactly [[null-span-score]].

So $s_{null}$ is not a separate formula. It is the same additive span score evaluated at the [CLS] position twice.

Which means a plain argmax over the widened candidate set would already answer or abstain, with no new machinery at all.

The paper does not do that. [[eq-null-answer-threshold]] first takes $\hat{s}_{i,j} = \max_{j \geq i} S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$ over real passage positions only. It then predicts that span only when $\hat{s}_{i,j} > s_{null} + \tau$.

Walk what [[tau-threshold]] does to the behaviour. At $\tau = 0$ the rule collapses back into the plain comparison. Push $\tau$ positive and a real span must now clear the null by a margin: abstentions go up, the answers that survive are the confident ones, and answers that would have been correct are given up. Push $\tau$ negative and the model answers even on questions where the null outscored every span.

One scalar, sliding the model along the answer-or-abstain trade-off after the fact.

Note how little the rule does. The null competes only against the single best span, not against a re-ranked list, and $\tau$ enters as a constant shift rather than as anything that depends on the question. It sits entirely outside [[span-prediction-head]], applied to two scalars once all the $H$-dimensional arithmetic is finished.

chapters.title: One scalar the gradient cannot reach
chapters.body:
The objective and the metric are measuring different things, and that is the whole reason $\tau$ exists.

The objective is the summed log-likelihood of the correct start and end. It is a statement about probability mass. It has no opinion about which kind of mistake is worse. A model that puts its start mass on the wrong passage token and a model that puts it on the passage when it should have abstained are both charged only for the mass that missed the gold index.

[[f1-score]] does have an opinion. On [[squad-v1-1]], [[exact-match-and-f1]] gives partial credit for token overlap, so a nearly-right span still earns something. On v2.0 an unanswerable question admits no partial credit: the model either abstains or it does not. So one of the two decisions is scored all-or-nothing and the other by overlap, and the likelihood cannot express that difference.

Fitting $\tau$ afterwards is how the paper closes the gap.

It cannot be closed by descent. F1 over a finite dev set is a step function of $\tau$: move $\tau$ a little and nothing changes until it crosses one question's margin, at which point that single question flips. The derivative is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the jumps.

The paper says only that $\tau$ is selected on dev to maximise F1. No procedure, no range, no sensitivity is reported. Because F1 is piecewise constant, sweeping the sorted margins would be exact and cheap, but the paper does not say that is what was run.

This is [[dev-set-model-selection]] doing the job it does throughout [[fine-tuning-bert]] — the same split that picks among [[fine-tuning-random-restarts]] also picks $\tau$. Dev F1 is therefore optimistic by construction. One weak counterweight: dev F1 is 81.9 and test F1 is 83.1, so no dev-fitting penalty shows up, though the two splits are not calibrated to equal difficulty.

chapters.title: What Table 3 settles and what it leaves open
chapters.body:
[[table-3]] is short enough to read row by row. Human performance: 86.9 EM, 89.5 F1 on test. The top leaderboard systems as of December 10th, 2018: MIR-MRC (F-Net) at 74.8 / 78.0, nlnet at 74.2 / 77.1. The published entries: unet as an ensemble at 71.4 / 74.9, SLQA+ as a single model at 71.4 / 74.4. Then a single [[bert-base-and-bert-large]] BERT_LARGE: 78.7 / 81.9 on dev, 80.0 / 83.1 on test.

The headline is $83.1 - 78.0 = 5.1$, an [[absolute-improvement]] over the strongest leaderboard entry. Against the best *published* system the same subtraction gives 8.2 points, and that entry is an ensemble while BERT's is one model. The caption names one exclusion: systems using BERT as a component are left out.

Against human 89.5 the model is 6.4 points short.

The recipe is stated in one line: 2 epochs, learning rate 5e-5, batch size 48, no TriviaQA. Set that beside v1.1's 3 epochs, 5e-5 and batch 32 with [[triviaqa-augmentation]]. Batch 48 sits outside the 16-or-32 range given in [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]], and no reason is offered. [[fine-tuning-cost]] still applies: this is hours, not days.

The comparison also inherits [[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules]] — those entries may train on any public data and have no current public descriptions. The caveat the paper raises itself for [[table-2]] applies here too, minus the augmentation it used there to answer it.

What the table does not establish. One model, one run, no variance. No ablation on $\tau$, so nothing separates how much of the 5.1 comes from the null-span construction and how much from the fitted threshold. No split of the score into answerable and [[unanswerable-questions]]. Nothing about how [[prior-squad-systems]] handle abstention.

n-eleven-tasks-and-the-numbers--squad-la.title: The 1.5, the 1.3, and the fine print
n-eleven-tasks-and-the-numbers--squad-la.intro: The parent read the margins off the table. This level reads the conditions the table was produced under: what the leaderboard actually permits, what TriviaQA fine-tuning is made of, which column the 0.1-0.4 was measured in, what the replaced architectures were doing, and what the human row is worth.

chapters.title: Two concessions, one footnote
chapters.body:
Section 4.2 hands over the board's terms in one sentence, and that sentence contains two separate admissions.

The first is about description. The top entries on [[squad-v1-1]] "do not have up-to-date public system descriptions available". A row is a name and a number.

The second is about data. Those entries "are allowed to use any public data when training their systems". Nothing fixes a common training set.

Together these are [[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules]]. Footnote 11 then narrows the second-place case: QANet is described in a published paper, but the system "has improved substantially after publication". So the one entry with a method attached has a method that no longer produces the number printed beside it.

Follow that through. The 91.7 and the 90.5 in [[table-2]] are measurements of systems whose current form cannot be inspected. A margin computed against them is a margin against a closed box.

The three leaderboard rows also carry Test figures only. Both Dev cells are dashes, on both of [[exact-match-and-f1]].

BERT's own ensemble row is specified, in the caption rather than the text: seven systems using different pre-training checkpoints and fine-tuning seeds. So [[ensembling]] here means averaging one recipe over its own randomness, not combining seven designs.

Only one of the two concessions admits a response. A method you cannot read cannot be matched. A data allowance can be. That is why the paper's answer takes the form it does, and why the description gap is simply left standing over the headline [[question-answering]] result.

chapters.title: Four hundred tokens, filtered by string match
chapters.body:
[[triviaqa-augmentation]] is described in the body as "modest data augmentation", and specified in footnote 12.

The data used is paragraphs from TriviaQA-Wiki, formed of the first 400 tokens in documents, kept only when the document contains at least one of the provided possible answers.

Two filters, then. Truncate each document to its opening 400 tokens. Discard it unless one of the listed answer strings survives inside that window.

What comes out has SQuAD's shape: a question, a passage, and at least one place in the passage that can be labelled as an [[answer-span]]. That is what makes it fine-tunable with the same head.

Notice how the span is found. It is found by string containment against a list of possible answers. It is not an annotator's judgement that this particular occurrence is the one the question asks about. The supervision is a match, and some matches will be the wrong occurrence.

The 400 is not explained, but it sits inside the model's limits. The input is a [[packed-question-passage-sequence]] — question, passage, special tokens — and pre-training was built around a [[max-sequence-length-512]]. Four hundred passage tokens leaves room for the question.

The two stages run in order, not jointly: fine-tune on TriviaQA, then fine-tune on SQuAD. The SQuAD stage is the one whose settings the section reports — three epochs, learning rate 5e-5, batch size 32, one point in the standard [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] grid.

So the reply to the data clause is a second supervised stage on a different [[token-level-tasks]] dataset. It matches the allowance rather than contesting it.

chapters.title: Which column the 0.1 to 0.4 lives in
chapters.body:
The paper says that without TriviaQA it loses only 0.1-0.4 F1. The table lets you locate most of that.

The two rows without TriviaQA carry Dev numbers and nothing else. Single BERT_LARGE reads 84.1 EM and 90.9 [[f1-score]] on Dev. The ensemble reads 85.8 and 91.8.

Now subtract against their TriviaQA counterparts. Single: $91.1 - 90.9 = 0.2$. Ensemble: $92.2 - 91.8 = 0.4$.

That is 0.2 and 0.4, not 0.1 and 0.4. The 0.1 does appear, but in the EM column: $84.2 - 84.1 = 0.1$. From the F1 columns alone the lower end of the quoted range cannot be found.

A second thing follows from those dashes. The claim that the non-augmented models still beat all existing systems compares a [[dev-set-model-selection]] number against Test numbers, because that is all the table holds on each side.

Is that comparison flattering? The two [[prior-squad-systems]] rows with both columns filled suggest not. BiDAF+ELMo goes 85.6 Dev to 85.8 Test. R.M. Reader goes 87.9 to 88.5. Both rise slightly when they cross.

Watch one coincidence while reading down the page: 91.8 appears twice in the table, once as a Dev F1 and once as a Test F1, for two different systems.

The remaining gap is variance. The ensemble exists because fine-tuning seeds and checkpoints differ from run to run. No spread is reported for any single row, so a 0.2 arrives with no error bar beside it. [[fine-tuning-cost]] is under an hour per run, which makes that absence a choice rather than a constraint.

chapters.title: What the published block had built
chapters.body:
The published baselines were not general encoders. They were reading-comprehension designs.

Section 3.2 names the pattern they share. Encode the two texts independently, then apply [[bidirectional-cross-attention]] between them: every question word attends over the passage, every passage word attends back over the question. BiDAF is cited as an instance. BiDAF+ELMo is that machine with [[elmo]] vectors fed in as extra input features, which makes it an instance of the [[feature-based-approach]] feeding a [[task-specific-architecture]].

BERT's counter-argument is [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention]]. Run [[self-attention]] over the concatenation and no distinction exists between a question-to-passage pair and a passage-to-passage pair. Every layer already computes both.

Price the difference in parameters. The [[span-prediction-head]] adds [[start-and-end-vectors]], one $S$ and one $E$, each of dimension $H$. For BERT_LARGE, [[bert-base-and-bert-large]] fixes $H = 1024$, so $2 \times 1024 = 2048$ new numbers sit on top of 340 million pre-trained ones. [[eq-span-start-probability]] is the whole added layer. That is [[minimal-task-specific-parameters]] taken about as far as it goes.

Be careful about what supports the claim. Section 3.2 asserts the subsumption, and the leaderboard row is consistent with it. No experiment stacks an explicit cross-attention layer on top of BERT to show that it adds nothing.

So the 3.3 F1 over the best published row shows that the stripped-down setup wins. It does not isolate the cross-attention machinery as the redundant part.

chapters.title: What 91.2 licenses
chapters.body:
The human row reads 82.3 Test EM and 91.2 Test F1. The table prints it, and the section text never mentions it.

BERT's single system with TriviaQA sits above both figures: 85.1 against 82.3, and 91.8 against 91.2. The ensemble sits further above, at 87.4 and 93.2.

But BERT is not the first row past it. nlnet's 86.0 EM clears 82.3, and its 91.7 F1 clears 91.2. QANet clears the human EM at 84.5 while falling short on F1 at 90.5. By December 10th 2018 the top of the board had already crossed the human line, on one metric at least.

R.M. Reader's Test EM is 82.3 exactly, equal to the human figure.

So the human row is not a frontier this paper breaks. It is a horizontal line that several systems had already reached.

The paper's restraint fits that. Every claim in the section is phrased against systems rather than against people, and [[state-of-the-art]] is the standard the whole [[eleven-task-evaluation]] is measured by.

The next section shows why the restraint is well placed. [[squad-v2-0]] adds [[unanswerable-questions]], and in [[table-3]] the human row is 89.5 F1 while the same fine-tuned model reaches 83.1. On the harder version the model is 6.4 behind.

Whatever the human row measures, it moves with the task definition. A system above it on one version can sit well below it on the next.
