n-what-each-piece-is-worth--frozen-encod.title: The masking mixture, row by row
n-what-each-piece-is-worth--frozen-encod.intro: The parent read Table 8 by column. This node reads it by row: what each of the three strategies actually removes from the model's available shortcuts, what the 80/10/10 split buys arithmetically, and how far the two extreme rows fall once you check them against every column rather than one.

chapters.title: What each strategy takes away
chapters.body:
Start with what the model actually sees.

Under [[masked-language-model|the masked LM objective]], a training example is a token sequence in which [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% of the positions]] have been drawn at random for prediction. The loss is computed only at those positions. Nothing in the input tells the model which positions they are.

That last point is what makes the three cases differ.

[[mask-same-rnd-strategies|MASK, SAME and RND]] each put something different in the chosen slot, and each closes off a different shortcut.

MASK writes [[mask-token|the placeholder]] into the slot. The placeholder is not a word, so it works as a flag: wherever it appears a prediction is wanted, and wherever it does not, none is. A model trained only this way is free to specialise — form a vocabulary distribution at flagged slots, and do as it likes at the rest.

SAME leaves the original token in place and asks for that same token back. Locally the job is a copy. But a SAME position is indistinguishable from an ordinary unselected position, so the only safe policy is to keep a usable prediction everywhere.

RND writes a random vocabulary item into the slot and still asks for the original. Now the visible token is evidence, and it is wrong. Copying the input is penalised.

SAME and RND therefore push in opposite directions. SAME rewards trusting the token you can see. RND forbids it.

The scored quantity is identical in all three cases. [[final-hidden-vector-ti|The top-layer vector at that position]] goes through [[mlm-output-softmax|the output softmax]] over [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|the 30,000 WordPiece types]], trained with cross-entropy against the original token.

chapters.title: The six runs, and what was not run
chapters.body:
[[table-8|The table]] gives six rows, three probability columns that sum to 100 in each, and three result columns. Read in order, the rows show that this is not a grid search.

Row one is [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|the shipped recipe]] at 80/10/10. It scores 84.2 on [[mnli]], 95.4 on fine-tuned [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]], and 94.9 frozen.

Row two is 100/0/0 — the placeholder every time: 84.3, 94.9, 94.0.

Row three is 80/0/20, the shipped recipe with its SAME share handed to RND: 84.1, 95.2, 94.6.

Row four is 80/20/0, the mirror image, SAME taking RND's share: 84.4, 95.2, 94.7.

Rows five and six remove MASK altogether. 0/20/80 gives 83.7, 94.8, 94.6. 0/0/100 gives 83.6, 94.9, 94.6.

So the runs fall into two families. Four hold MASK at 80% or 100% and redistribute what is left. Two set MASK to zero.

Nothing between the families is sampled. There is no row at 50% MASK, none at 20%. Whatever the curve does as the placeholder share falls from 80 to 0, only its two ends are measured here.

The result columns are all Dev numbers, read off [[dev-set-model-selection|the development split]]. MNLI is accuracy after fine-tuning. The first NER column is [[f1-score|F1]] after fine-tuning. The second is F1 with the encoder frozen, features taken by [[concat-last-four-layers|concatenating the top four hidden layers]], which is what [[layer-selection-ablation|the layer comparison]] had found best. Everything outside the three probabilities is presented as unchanged, though the appendix does not restate [[pre-training-procedure|the recipe]] these runs used.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

chapters.title: The 80/10/10 split, counted out
chapters.body:
[[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|The mismatch]] the split was designed against is easiest to see as a count of slots.

Take a 128-token sequence, the length used for most of pre-training under [[sequence-length-schedule|the two-stage length schedule]]. Fifteen percent of 128 is about 19 positions selected for prediction. Eighty percent of those 19 is about 15 placeholders. Ten percent each leaves roughly 2 random tokens and 2 untouched tokens.

Now the downstream side. A [[fine-tuning-bert|fine-tuning]] input contains no placeholders at all. So a pre-training input and a fine-tuning input differ in about 15 of 128 slots — call it one [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]] in eight.

Under 100/0/0 that would be 19 in 128, and every scored position would be flagged.

The split does not close that gap. What it changes is what the flag licenses the model to infer. Two of the 19 scored positions carry their true token, so a real word present no longer means "not scored". Two more carry a wrong token, so a real word present no longer means "correct". Two inferences blocked, at the price of 4 positions in 19.

One limit is worth stating. Those SAME and RND slots still sit inside a sequence holding roughly 15 placeholders. The slot matches downstream conditions; its context does not.

The paper's own verbs are "mitigate" and "reduce", never remove.

And because BERT scores only the selected positions rather than reconstructing everything — [[denoising-autoencoder-contrast|unlike a denoising autoencoder]] — those 19 slots carry the whole [[masked-language-model|masked-LM]] signal. Changing the mixture changes all of it, not a fraction.

chapters.title: How far MASK-only actually falls
chapters.body:
Now put numbers on [[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|the amplification claim]].

On fine-tuned NER, the shipped mixture reads 95.4 and MASK-only reads 94.9. That is a drop of 0.5. Frozen, the same two rows read 94.9 and 94.0, a drop of 0.9. Roughly double.

The sharper reading is not the ratio but the ranking.

In the fine-tuned NER column, 94.9 is not the lowest score in the table — the 0/20/80 row sits at 94.8. So MASK-only cannot be picked out of that column at all; it is somewhere in the middle of a 0.6-point spread.

In the frozen column it sits alone. The other five rows occupy 94.6 to 94.9. MASK-only at 94.0 is 0.6 below the nearest of them.

The frozen column is the only place the row separates.

The mechanism offered for that is a matter of which parameters can move. In [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|the frozen setting]] the twelve encoder layers are fixed. Only [[frozen-feature-bilstm-classifier|the two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM]] and the tag classifier train, reading [[first-sub-token-classification|the first sub-token's vector]] under [[tagging-without-crf|a plain per-token output layer]]. If the encoder has learned to key its behaviour on a placeholder that downstream text never contains, nothing above it can reach inside and retune that. The [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuning route]], with [[end-to-end-fine-tuning|every parameter moving]], can.

How strong is this? It is one row, one task, one dataset, one number. The direction matches the prediction. The size of the effect rests on a single 0.9-point comparison, and the appendix reports no variance for it.

chapters.title: The RND rows, and what the table can carry
chapters.body:
[[masking-procedure-ablation|The appendix]] closes by calling RND-only "much worse than our strategy as well". Check that against all three columns.

RND-only reads 83.6 MNLI, 94.9 fine-tuned NER, 94.6 frozen NER. Frozen, it is 0.3 off the shipped mixture and level with two other rows. Fine-tuned NER puts it level with MASK-only. Neither NER column marks it out.

MNLI does. At 83.6 it is the lowest of the six.

And it is not alone there. The other zero-MASK row, 0/20/80, reads 83.7. The four rows that keep MASK span 84.1 to 84.4. So the two no-MASK runs are the bottom two on MNLI, 0.4 to 0.8 behind the rest.

That is the one pattern in the table that tracks a mixture variable across more than a single row. The appendix does not point at it — its RND sentence sits in a paragraph about the frozen setting, where RND-only is unremarkable.

Note also that MASK-only, the row called problematic, is second-best on MNLI at 84.3.

On footing: [[table-7|the main NER table]] states that its scores are averaged over five restarts, a precaution [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|taken because fine-tuning could be unstable]]. Table 8's one-line caption says nothing about restarts, model size, or [[training-steps-and-epochs|training length]].

Whole-table spreads are 0.8 on MNLI, 0.6 and 0.9 on NER. With no variance reported, a 0.1 or 0.3 [[absolute-improvement|point difference]] cannot be separated from run-to-run noise here. "Fine-tuning is surprisingly robust" is the claim this [[ablation-studies|ablation]] can carry.
